title: One bowl, six tastes: how traditional and festival meals balance a diet

summary.text: At Ugadi, many families in Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana start the year with a pachadi that holds six tastes in one bowl: sweet jaggery, sour tamarind, salt, bitter neem flowers, hot pepper and raw mango. Why would a festival dish contain a bitter flower? Your child tests the school-book 'tongue map' with a blind taste test, and finds that every taste can be felt all over the tongue. They sprout moong and time how long each batch takes to cook, to see what soaking and sprouting change in a food. They plan a balanced festival feast from many parts of India, keep a seven-day food diary, and find out why a sweet taste does not always mean a food is good for the body.
summary.art: A steel bowl of Ugadi pachadi on a banana leaf, with six small piles beside it: jaggery, tamarind, salt, neem flowers, black pepper and raw mango pieces.

intro.hook: Look at a spoon of Ugadi pachadi. It holds sweet jaggery, sour tamarind, salt, bitter neem flowers, hot pepper and raw mango. All six are in one spoon. Why would anyone put a bitter flower in a festival dish?
intro.text: Many traditional meals look as if someone planned them. A Kerala sadya on a banana leaf can have twenty dishes, and each dish has its own place on the leaf. A Gujarati thali has roti, dal, rice, a vegetable, buttermilk and something sweet. Nobody wrote these meals from a nutrition book. Yet they hold grains, pulses, vegetables and milk, and a mix of tastes. So how does a meal become balanced? And is a tasty meal always a balanced one? In this unit you test your own tongue, soak and sprout some moong seeds, and plan a festival feast.
intro.art: A Kerala sadya on a banana leaf seen from above, with many small dishes in rows, and a girl pointing at the bitter pavakka dish.

outcomes: I can explain that a balanced diet is a pattern of many kinds of food over days, not one perfect plate and not one magic food.
I can sort the dishes of a traditional meal into energy-giving, body-building and protective foods, and spot which group is missing.
I can name the six tastes of shad rasa and the five tastes that science finds, and say how the two lists differ.
I can run a fair blind taste test and use the results to show that the tongue map in old books is wrong.
I can explain why a taste is a signal, and why a food can give the signal without giving the goodness.
I can explain how soaking, sprouting and fermenting change plant foods, and name some millets and why farmers grow them in dry land.
I can say why each festival has the foods it has, and why festival sweets suit special days better than every day.
I can plan one meal that works for people with different needs.

terms.meaning: The main food a region eats every day, which gives most of its energy. It is usually a grain or a root.
terms.example: Rice in Kerala, wheat in Punjab, ragi in parts of Karnataka and bajra in Rajasthan are staple foods.
terms.art: Four plates, each with a different staple: rice, roti, a ragi ball and a bajra roti.

terms.meaning: Eating many different foods across a day and a week, so that the body gets all the nutrients it needs.
terms.example: Dal, rice, a green vegetable, curd and a fruit on a plate is more variety than rice with a pickle.
terms.art: A week calendar with a different coloured food drawn on each day.

terms.meaning: A food or meal that families in a place have cooked and passed on for many generations.
terms.example: Idli with sambar in Tamil Nadu and makki roti with sarson saag in Punjab are traditional meals.
terms.art: A grandmother handing a rolling pin to a girl in a kitchen, with a recipe notebook open between them.

terms.meaning: A food that grows or is eaten in one part of the year.
terms.example: Raw mango is a summer food. Sesame and jaggery sweets are eaten in the cool months.
terms.art: A wheel of four seasons with a different food in each part: mango, sugarcane, til laddu and pumpkin.

terms.meaning: A tiny group of taste cells. Taste buds sit on your tongue, the roof of your mouth and the back of your throat.
terms.example: You have thousands of taste buds, and each one can sense more than one taste.
terms.art: A zoomed-in drawing of a tongue bump with one onion-shaped taste bud cut open to show its cells.

terms.meaning: The taste of savoury, 'meaty' foods. It was named in Japan in 1908 and is made by a chemical called glutamate.
terms.example: Ripe tomato, mushroom, cheese and a spoon of well-cooked dal all have umami.
terms.art: A bowl of dal with a ripe tomato and a mushroom next to the bowl, and the word umami on a small tag.

terms.meaning: The six tastes of Ayurveda, a very old Indian system of medicine: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent.
terms.example: Jaggery is sweet, tamarind is sour, salt is salty, chilli is pungent, neem is bitter and raw banana is astringent.
terms.art: Six small bowls in a circle, each holding one ingredient, with the name of its taste written under it.

terms.meaning: The hot, burning feeling of chilli, pepper and ginger. Science counts it as a feeling of heat and pain, not as a taste.
terms.example: Black pepper in venn pongal makes your tongue feel hot.
terms.art: A child fanning her open mouth beside a green chilli and a pile of black pepper.

terms.meaning: A dry, puckering feeling in the mouth, like a tight skin on the tongue. Science counts it as a feeling of touch.
terms.example: A raw banana, strong tea and an unripe guava all feel astringent.
terms.art: A girl biting a raw banana with her lips pulled tight.

terms.meaning: A small-seeded grain that grows well in dry land with little water. Ragi, jowar and bajra are millets.
terms.example: Ragi mudde in Karnataka, jowar roti in Maharashtra and bajra rotla in Gujarat are made from millets.
terms.art: Three jars of millet grains, ragi, jowar and bajra, with a small ear of each plant beside the jar.

terms.meaning: When a soaked seed wakes up and starts to grow a tiny root. A sprouted seed is alive and growing.
terms.example: Moong beans soaked and kept damp for a day send out small white tails.
terms.art: Three moong seeds in a row: dry, swollen from soaking, and with a small white tail.

terms.meaning: A food changed by living microbes, such as yeast and bacteria, into something new.
terms.example: Idli and dosa batter, curd and toddy are fermented foods.
terms.art: A steel pot of idli batter risen to the brim with bubbles on top.

terms.meaning: A packaged food made in a factory from refined ingredients, with added sugar, salt, fat, flavours or colours.
terms.example: Many chips, instant noodles, fizzy drinks and packet biscuits are ultra-processed foods.
terms.art: A shelf of brightly coloured packets of chips, noodles and biscuits beside a basket of fresh vegetables.

explanations.concept: A balanced diet is a pattern over many days
explanations.definition: A balanced diet is a mix of many different foods, eaten over days and weeks, that gives the body enough of every nutrient it needs.
explanations.description: In Class 3 you built a balanced plate. A plate is one meal. But the body does not need every meal to be perfect. You can eat very little greens at lunch and make up for it at dinner or tomorrow. What matters is the pattern over many days. No single food has everything the body needs. The one food that comes close is a mother's milk, for a baby in the first six months. After that, a body needs variety. Eating many kinds of grain, pulse, vegetable, fruit and milk food helps, because each one carries a different mix of nutrients. A balanced diet is also not the same for everyone. A growing child, a grandmother, a runner and a pregnant woman need different amounts. The Indian Council of Medical Research and its National Institute of Nutrition, in Hyderabad, publish the Dietary Guidelines for Indians that families can use.
examples: A child who eats dal, a green vegetable and curd at lunch can have a lighter dinner, and still be balanced over the day.
A family that eats only rice and potato for a week is not balanced, even if each meal fills the stomach.
A pregnant woman needs more iron than other adults, so her plate holds more greens, pulses and iron-rich foods.
explanations.art: A week calendar with seven plates, each different, and a ring drawn round all seven to show that the whole week is the plate.

explanations.concept: Traditional meals are balanced in their own way
explanations.definition: A traditional meal is a set of dishes that people in a region have long eaten together. Many of them join a staple food, a pulse, a vegetable and a milk food.
explanations.description: Meals in different parts of India look different, but they do the same job. In Tamil Nadu a meal is rice, sambar or rasam, a vegetable, curd and a pickle. In Gujarat it is roti, dal, rice, a vegetable, buttermilk and a sweet. In Bengal it is rice, dal, fish or vegetables, and a bitter dish like shukto at the start. In Nagaland and Manipur it is rice, boiled leafy vegetables, and a chutney of chilli and fermented fish or bamboo shoot. In Punjab it is makki roti with sarson saag, butter and lassi. The dishes are different, but each plate has a staple for energy, a pulse or fish or milk for building, and vegetables for protection. These meals grew over many generations from what the land grew, and from families noticing which foods kept them strong. They were not planned from a table of nutrients, and they are not perfect. But they often work.
examples: A Kerala sadya joins rice, parippu, sambar, avial, thoran, pulissery, pickles and payasam on one banana leaf.
A Gujarati thali has bajra or wheat roti, dal, kadhi, a vegetable, rice and chaas.
A Hyderabadi biryani with raita joins rice, meat or vegetables, and curd.
explanations.art: Four plates side by side, a Tamil, a Gujarati, a Bengali and a Naga meal, each with the three food jobs marked by small coloured dots.

explanations.concept: Six tastes or five: two ways of sorting what the tongue tells us
explanations.description: Ayurveda, a very old Indian system of medicine, sorts food by six tastes, called shad rasa. They are sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent. The Charaka Samhita, a very old Ayurvedic text, describes them in its chapter on tastes. It teaches that a healthy meal holds all six. Taste scientists today find five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Each has its own kind of sensor on the taste cells. Pungent and astringent are missing from the science list, because they are not tastes. The heat of chilli is a signal of heat and pain. A dry, puckering mouth after raw banana is a signal of touch. The two lists do not match. But both are careful ways of sorting what a mouth tells us.
examples: Jaggery tastes sweet in both lists.
Chilli is pungent in shad rasa. In science it is a heat signal from nerves, not a taste.
Umami is on the science list but has no place in the six rasas.
explanations.art: Two lists side by side. On the left, the six rasas with an ingredient for each. On the right, five taste sensors, with arrows showing which rasas match.

perspectives.explanation: The six tastes are the main way a cook can see what a food will do in the body. A meal with all six keeps a person well. The tastes are tools for choosing food.

Taste is the work of five kinds of sensor on the taste cells. Chilli heat and the dry feel of tea come from nerves of touch and pain. The six rasas are a useful cook's list, but they are not a map of the tongue's sensors.

explanations.concept: The tongue map is wrong: every taste is sensed everywhere
explanations.definition: Taste cells for every taste are found all over the tongue, and also on the roof of the mouth and in the throat. There is no tongue map with one zone for each taste.
explanations.description: A tongue is covered in tiny bumps. Many of them hold taste buds. A taste bud is a small group of 50 to 100 taste cells, packed like segments of an orange. Each cell senses one kind of taste, and one bud can hold cells for several. A taste cell lives only about ten days to two weeks, and then a new one grows. So your sense of taste is being rebuilt all the time. The old tongue map taught that the tip tastes sweet and the back tastes bitter. In fact, all the tastes are sensed in all the zones. The zones differ a little in how sensitive they are. The middle of the tongue has fewer taste buds, so it is a little less sensitive. But there is no zone that is blind to a taste.
examples: A drop of lemon water on the tip of the tongue tastes sour, and so does a drop at the back.
Salt on the tip is salty, even though the old map put salt on the sides.
When you burn your tongue on hot tea, the taste buds are damaged, and new ones grow back within about two weeks.
explanations.art: A tongue seen from above with five coloured dots on every zone, and a crossed-out old map beside it.

explanations.concept: Taste is a signal about what is in the food
explanations.description: Why do we have taste at all? One idea is that each taste is a message about what is in the food. Sweet tells you there is sugar, a quick fuel. Salty tells you there are minerals the body needs for its nerves and water balance. Sour is the taste of acids, in unripe fruit, in lemon and amla, and in food that has started to go bad. Bitter warns of food that may be poisonous, because many poisons in plants are bitter. Umami tells you there is protein. This fits what babies do. Newborns make a relaxed, almost smiling face for sweet and a screwed-up face for bitter, before they have eaten anything. But it is only an idea. Taste is not a perfect guide. Some bitter foods, like karela and neem, are good for us in small amounts, and some poisons taste sweet. We also learn tastes. A baby tastes flavours of the mother's food in the womb and in her milk, and later likes those flavours more. Julie Mennella, a scientist in the USA, showed this in the 1990s and 2000s.
examples: Children who are given a little karela many times often learn to like it, because bitter can be learned.
A very ripe mango tastes sweet and a little sour, which tells you it holds sugar and acid.
A rotten idli batter tastes sharply sour, which is why we do not eat it.
explanations.art: A tongue in the centre with five arrows pointing to icons: a sugar cube, a salt crystal, a lemon, a bitter gourd with a warning sign, and a bowl of dal.

explanations.concept: A taste can be copied without the goodness
explanations.definition: A taste is a signal from the chemicals in a food. A food can give the signal without the goodness that used to come with it.
explanations.description: A ripe mango gives sweetness together with fibre, vitamins and water. A bottle of sweet fizzy drink gives the same sweet signal with sugar and almost nothing else. Your tongue cannot tell the difference. It only reports sweet. Long ago, sweet foods were rare, mostly fruit and honey. A body that loved sweet was well fed. Today a factory can add sugar, salt and fat to a packet of chips or biscuits. The signal is strong, so we want more, but the food does not give the goodness. The World Health Organization advises that sugars added to food and drink should be less than one tenth of the energy we eat in a day. Some foods are made so that eating them is hard to stop. That is why one packet of chips is rarely enough.
examples: A sweet fizzy drink gives sugar and no fibre, no protein and almost no vitamins.
Instant noodle flavour packets give a strong salty signal and little else.
A guava gives sweetness together with fibre and a lot of vitamin C.
explanations.art: Two glasses side by side, a mango lassi with a mango beside it and a fizzy drink with a pile of sugar cubes, both with a big sweet arrow.

explanations.concept: Festival foods: made from the season, rich in energy, made to share
explanations.definition: A festival food is a dish made for a special day. Many of them use what the season gives, are rich in energy, and keep well or feed many people.
explanations.description: Festival foods follow the year. Pongal in January is cooked from the new rice harvest, with jaggery from sugarcane, moong dal and ghee. Makar Sankranti is in the cool months, and in Maharashtra people give til-gul, sesame with jaggery, which is rich in fat and energy. Ugadi is in spring, when raw mango and neem flowers come, so the pachadi is made of them. Onam is at the end of the monsoon, and its sadya is full of vegetables, banana and coconut. Diwali sweets and savouries, like laddu and murukku, have a lot of sugar and oil and very little water. Microbes cannot grow in food with little water, so these keep for weeks and can be shared. Many festival foods are rich in sugar and ghee because the day is special. Eaten on a few days of the year, they fit into a balanced diet. Eaten every day, they would not.
examples: Pongal: new rice, moong dal, jaggery and ghee, cooked in a new pot.
Til-gul in Maharashtra at Makar Sankranti: sesame and jaggery, for the cool months.
Diwali murukku and laddu, which keep for weeks because they have little water.
explanations.art: A wheel of the year with five festival foods placed on it: Pongal, til-gul, Ugadi pachadi, Onam sadya and Diwali sweets.

explanations.concept: Millets: very old grains with new attention
explanations.definition: Millets are small-seeded grasses grown as grain. Ragi, jowar, bajra, kodo, little millet and foxtail millet are all millets.
explanations.description: People in India have grown millets for thousands of years. They grow in dry land with little water and little care. Ragi is rich in calcium, and has far more than rice does. Bajra and jowar bring fibre and iron. Fibre slows down how fast the body takes in sugar, and feeds the microbes in the gut. After the Green Revolution of the 1960s, India grew far more rice and wheat, and less millet. Rice and wheat were given at ration shops and became the grains everyone knew. Now millets are getting attention again. The United Nations marked 2023 as the International Year of Millets, which India had asked for. Advertisements sometimes call millets a superfood. 'Superfood' is a selling word, not a science word. Millets are good food, but no single food gives the body everything.
examples: Ragi mudde and ragi dosa in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
Jowar roti in Maharashtra and Karnataka, and bajra rotla in Gujarat.
Samai, thinai and varagu in Tamil Nadu are the names for little millet, foxtail millet and kodo millet.
explanations.art: A dry field with three millet plants, ragi, jowar and bajra, each with their ear of grain, and a cloud of rain far off.

explanations.concept: Old ways of preparing food: soaking, sprouting, fermenting and a squeeze of lemon
explanations.definition: Soaking, sprouting and fermenting are ways of preparing plant foods that make the minerals inside them easier for the body to take in.
explanations.description: Grains, pulses and seeds hold a store of phosphorus in a chemical called phytic acid. Phytic acid holds on to iron, zinc and calcium, so the gut can take in less of them. When seeds are soaked and begin to sprout, they wake up and make enzymes that break phytic acid down. The same happens, more slowly, when microbes ferment the batter for idli and dosa. Sprouting also makes a little vitamin C, which dry seeds do not have. A squeeze of lemon on greens or dal adds vitamin C that helps the gut take in iron from plant foods. Tea and coffee drunk with a meal do the opposite, and can lower how much iron is taken in. This is why guides for Indian families say to leave an hour between a meal and tea. Families found these ways by trying, long before anyone knew about phytic acid. Hotz and Gibson wrote about this in 2007.
examples: Soaking dal for an hour or two before cooking, or soaking rajma overnight.
Idli and dosa batter that is left to ferment overnight.
A squeeze of lemon on palak or on sprouts.
explanations.art: Four small scenes in a row: moong seeds soaking in a bowl, sprouts in a damp cloth, risen idli batter, and a lemon being squeezed over palak.

explanations.concept: Food is not shared equally: too little and too much
explanations.definition: Some children do not get enough food or enough of the right foods, and others eat too much of foods that are high in sugar, fat and salt. Both are called malnutrition.
explanations.description: India grows more food than it needs, and yet many people do not eat a balanced diet. The National Family Health Survey, done in 2019 to 2021, found that more than a third of children under five were too short for their age, and that more than half of women aged 15 to 49 had anaemia, a shortage of iron in the blood. At the same time, more children than before were overweight. The reason is not a shortage of food. It is about money, work, how far a market is, what is sold in shops, and who in the family eats first and last. Free school meals are one answer. Tamil Nadu began giving meals to children in schools in the 1950s, and a national scheme now serves them across India. Studies have found that school meals bring more children to school, as well as feeding them.
examples: A midday meal of rice, dal and a vegetable can be the biggest meal of the day for a child.
A family with less money buys more rice and less milk, fruit and pulses, because rice fills the stomach at lower cost.
A child in a city who eats packets and fizzy drinks every day can be overweight and short of iron at the same time.
explanations.art: Two children side by side: one eating a midday meal of rice, dal and vegetables on a steel plate, and one holding a packet of chips and a fizzy drink.

explanations.concept: People taste the same food differently
explanations.description: Ask a class to taste a piece of raw karela. Some will say it is very bitter and some will say it is only a little bitter. Scientists think part of this comes from genes. Bitter taste cells use many kinds of sensor, and the genes for these sensors are a little different from person to person. In 1931 Arthur Fox, a chemist in the USA, let a powder called PTC float into the air. A colleague nearby said it tasted bitter, and Fox tasted nothing. People turned out to fall into two groups, those who taste PTC as bitter and those who do not, and the difference comes from a gene. Experience matters too. A child who grows up eating karela often finds it less harsh. So when two people taste the same food and disagree, are they tasting different things, or tasting differently? Scientists would say a bit of both. The food is the same, but each tongue and each past is different.
examples: One person finds coriander leaves fresh, and another finds them soapy. Part of this comes from genes.
A person who grew up on fermented bamboo shoot may enjoy a smell that a visitor finds strong.
Two cousins eat the same pachadi, and one calls the neem too bitter while the other asks for more.
explanations.art: Two children tasting the same piece of karela, one wincing and one smiling, with a small DNA strand drawn above each head.

agreed.text: A balanced diet is a mix of many foods over days, not one perfect plate and not one magic food.
agreed.evidence: The ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) are built on this idea. Studies of food variety and health across many countries point the same way.

agreed.text: Every basic taste can be sensed on every part of the tongue that has taste buds.
agreed.evidence: In 1974 Virginia Collings tested people carefully and found this. Later, scientists found the sensor proteins on taste cells all over the tongue (Chandrashekar and colleagues, Nature, 2006).

agreed.text: Soaking, sprouting and fermenting grains and pulses can make it easier for the body to take in iron and zinc.
agreed.evidence: These steps lower phytic acid in the food. Hotz and Gibson reviewed the studies in the Journal of Nutrition in 2007.

agreed.text: Millets are nutritious grains that grow in dry land with little water.
agreed.evidence: The Indian Food Composition Tables (2017) list their fibre and minerals, and the Indian Institute of Millets Research in Hyderabad studies how they grow.

agreed.text: Eating a lot of sugar, salt and fat in packaged food, day after day, goes with eating more energy than the body needs.
agreed.evidence: In a 2019 study by Kevin Hall and colleagues, adults eating mostly ultra-processed food ate about 500 kilocalories more each day than when they ate unprocessed food.

agreed.text: Many children and women in India are short of iron and other nutrients, even though India grows enough food.
agreed.evidence: The National Family Health Survey 2019 to 2021 measured anaemia and the height of young children in every state.

challenging.claim: Each taste has its own zone on the tongue, with sweet at the tip and bitter at the back.
challenging.who: This 'tongue map' was drawn in a book in 1942 and then copied into school books for decades.
challenging.for: Some zones are a little more sensitive to some tastes. The tip is quite good at sweet, and the back is quite good at bitter.
challenging.against: In 1974 Virginia Collings, and many scientists after her, found that every taste is sensed in every zone. The differences are small. In the Blind Taste Test, you can check this on your own tongue.

challenging.claim: Traditional food is always healthier than modern food.
challenging.who: Many people, in advertisements and in conversations about old and new ways of eating.
challenging.for: Many traditional meals are built on whole foods, with a staple, a pulse, vegetables and often fermented foods. Old ways of soaking, sprouting and fermenting do help.
challenging.against: Some traditional diets lacked certain nutrients. A diet of mostly polished rice has little thiamine. Some festival foods are very rich in sugar and ghee. Tradition is a good start, but it needs checking.

challenging.claim: If you crave a food, your body needs what is in it.
challenging.who: A common belief, and sometimes an argument in diet books.
challenging.for: The body does have a real hunger for salt when it is short of it. Some people crave soil or ice when they are short of iron.
challenging.against: Most cravings for sweet or salty snacks come from habit, mood and factory food that is made to be hard to stop. A craving for a packet of biscuits does not mean the body needs biscuits.

challenging.claim: Millets are a new 'superfood' that fixes diets.
challenging.for: Millets are rich in fibre and minerals, and ragi is rich in calcium.
challenging.against: Millets are not new, and 'superfood' is not a science word. No single food gives the body everything. A dish made of millet with a lot of sugar and oil is not a health food.

challenging.claim: Festival sweets are bad and should be avoided.
challenging.who: Some health writers, and some families that worry about sugar.
challenging.for: Sweets are rich in sugar, and a lot of sugar every day is linked to health problems.
challenging.against: A balanced diet is about the pattern over weeks. A laddu on Diwali or a payasam on Onam fits into a pattern that is mostly varied whole food. Sharing festival food also has value for a family.

big_questions.q: When you taste a bitter karela and your friend says it is not bitter, are you tasting different things, or tasting differently?
big_questions.hint: Think about the food, the tongue, the genes and the past, and which of them differs between you.

big_questions.q: Where does a meal end and you begin?
big_questions.hint: Think about the rice you ate last week, the cells in your body, and the days it takes for food to become part of you.

big_questions.q: A sweet drink gives the same sweet signal as a mango, but not the same goodness. What else might your senses tell you that is not the whole story?
big_questions.hint: Think of a colour that looks different to a bee, or a smell that is strong to a dog and weak to you.

big_questions.q: Every region of India built a balanced meal from different foods. What does that tell us about what a balanced diet really is?
big_questions.hint: Compare a Kerala sadya, a Gujarati thali and a Naga meal. What do they share?

big_questions.q: India grows enough food, yet many children go without a balanced meal. What would make meals fairer?
big_questions.hint: Think about money, markets, school meals and who eats first in a home.

big_questions.q: Almost every culture marks special days with special food. Why might sharing food matter so much to people?
big_questions.hint: Think about who cooks, who is invited, and what does not happen on an ordinary day.

big_questions.q: Traditional cooks in the past found that soaking and fermenting helped, without knowing about phytic acid. How can people know something works before they know why?
big_questions.hint: Think about how a family learns a recipe, and what a test adds to a recipe.

big_questions.q: Is a taste in the food, in the tongue, or in the brain?
big_questions.hint: Think about the same sugar tasting sweet to you, and what a bee or a cat would sense from the same sugar.

story.title: Bevu-Bella
story.note: A made-up story, set in Mysuru at Ugadi. In Karnataka the neem-and-jaggery mix of Ugadi is called bevu-bella. The science in it is real. Tastes are sensed all over the tongue, smell is sensed by the nose, and a loss of smell after an illness is real and often comes back slowly. Nandini, Ajji and the family are made up.
text: In Mysuru, everyone agreed that Ajji made the best Ugadi pachadi. She had made it every spring for fifty years. Nandini was in Class 4, and this year she was allowed to hold the bowl.

But this year Ajji was not herself. In February she had a long fever. The fever went, and she got up, and she walked to the market again. Yet she sat on the kitchen cot with her hands in her lap, looking at the pots.

'Nothing smells,' she told Nandini. 'Not the jasmine, not the coffee, not the rasam. Yesterday I put my nose over the rasam pot, and it was like an empty pot.' She took a spoon of last week's rasam and tasted it. 'Sour? Salt? I cannot tell. A cook with no tongue. Better to buy the pachadi from the shop.'

Nandini looked at the brass plate. On it lay the six things Ajji always used: a lump of jaggery, a ball of tamarind, a pinch of salt, a few tiny neem flowers, some black pepper and a raw mango. 'Six tastes in one bowl,' Ajji always said. 'Life will have all six this year, so we taste them all on the first day.'
Nandini remembered something from her notebook. 'Ajji,' she said slowly. 'I think your tongue is still working. Can I test it?'
'Test an old tongue?' Ajji laughed, for the first time that week. 'Go on, then.'

Nandini set out four steel katoris. One had sugar water, one salt water, one lemon water, and one plain water. 'Plain water is the catch,' she explained. 'If you say sweet to plain water, you are only guessing.' She hid the cups behind a tray and shuffled them. Ajji shut her eyes and stuck out her tongue. Nandini dipped a clean cotton bud and touched the tip.
'Sweet,' said Ajji at once.
Nandini touched the side of the tongue with another bud. 'Salt.' She touched the very back. 'Sour! Oh, my cheeks!' Ajji's eyes flew open. 'But I can taste. I can taste!'
'You can,' said Nandini. 'The tongue tastes sweet, sour, salty and bitter. All of them, all over. What you lost is your smell. The smell is what makes a mango taste of mango.'
Ajji frowned. 'My teacher said the sweet is at the front and the bitter is at the back.'
'Try the sour at the front,' said Nandini. Ajji tried it. She made the same face. 'Hm,' she said. 'Fifty years I have been telling the children the wrong map.'

Then she went quiet again. 'But the pachadi is not about one taste,' she said. 'It is right only when no taste is the boss. Sweet, sour, salt, bitter, hot, raw. My nose always told me when it was right. Now I have no nose.'
Nandini opened her notebook to a clean page. 'Then we make a table,' she said. 'You use your tongue for each taste, one at a time, and I will write it down.'

They did it slowly. Nandini stirred a little jaggery into a spoon of water. Ajji tasted and said, 'Two.' It was Nandini's scale from the notebook, nought for nothing and three for very strong. She added the tamarind and Ajji said, 'Two.' The salt, 'Two.' Then the neem flowers, just three of them, for neem is strong. 'One. Add three more. Now two.' Then a pinch of pepper, 'Two, and it burns, so it is not really a taste, it is a fire.' Then the raw mango, cut small. 'Two, and my mouth goes dry.'
Nandini wrote six twos on the page. She mixed everything in the big bowl. Ajji tasted from the tip of the spoon, and then from the side, and then from the back. Her eyes filled.
'It is all there,' she said. 'Everything is there. But it has no smell. It is not my pachadi.'
Nandini's little brother Harsha, who was six, had sneaked in and was standing beside the cot with a spoon. He took a taste. His face went through everything, sweet, sour, then a scowl, then a grin.
'Ajji,' he said. 'It is like the whole year in one spoon.' He licked the spoon. 'Can I have more?'

Ajji looked at him, and then at the page of six twos in Nandini's handwriting. 'For fifty years my nose did the cooking, and my tongue only agreed,' she said. 'This year my tongue cooked, and my granddaughter was my notebook.' She took the spoon from Harsha and held it up. 'Bring me another bowl. Everyone must taste it.'
They ate the pachadi that evening, a spoonful each, with the festival meal. Nobody said it was not the same. Nobody said it was.

In June, Ajji was drinking her morning coffee when she stopped, with the steel tumbler halfway to her mouth. She did not say anything. She only closed her eyes and breathed in. Nandini wrote the date on the page in her notebook, under the six twos.
story.epiphany: Ajji's tongue was never gone. Every taste can be sensed all over the tongue. What she had lost was her sense of smell.
ask: Why did Nandini put a cup of plain water among the other cups?
Why was the pachadi right when all six tastes scored the same?
What would you do if you had to make a dish for someone who could not smell?

A girl touching a cotton bud to the tongue of her grandmother, who has her eyes shut, with four steel katoris on a tray.

roots.context: In this unit we tested the tongue, sprouted moong seeds and planned festival meals. Now we ask what these tell us about taste, about food, and about where a meal ends and we begin.

deep_truth.truth: Your tongue does not measure goodness. It reports sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami, which once pointed to energy, minerals, ripe fruit, danger and protein. A sweet drink can give the sweet report with none of the fruit. So wanting a taste is not the same as needing the food.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'it tastes good, so it is good for me', and we say 'I crave it, so my body needs it'. But taste is only a signal made by the food's chemicals. It was a good guide for whole foods, and a food made in a factory can copy the signal without the goodness.
deep_truth.evidence: In the blind taste test, a spoonful of sugar in water gave a clear sweet signal on every part of the tongue, though sugar water has no protein, fibre or vitamins. The pachadi sends six different signals from six different foods, and the tongue reads them all. The tongue tells you what is touching it, and says nothing about what the food will do inside you.

three.who_am_i: You are the one who tastes, and your taste is partly built from your genes, your mother's food and the meals you grew up on.
three.what_is_life: Your taste cells die and are replaced about every ten days to two weeks. So the part of you that tastes is being rebuilt all the time, from the food you eat.
three.what_is_this_world: A sweet fruit, a bitter leaf and a salty crystal are different chemicals, and living beings built a sense that reads each one as a message.

roots.thread: A bitter flower, a sweet lump of jaggery and a sour fruit are all made from the same few kinds of atoms, rearranged by plants using sunlight. Your tongue does not read atoms. It reads shapes of molecules, which fit its sensors like keys in locks. Then your brain turns those shapes into sweet, sour and bitter. So a taste is made when the food meets the one who tastes. The food was built by a plant. The tongue was built by a body, which came from other bodies before it, going back a very long way. When you eat, the food becomes part of your body.

teachings.teaching: The text says that all beings are born from food, live by food, and go back into food when they die. It calls food the first of all things, because it is what a living being is made of.
teachings.link: Your tongue, your blood and your bones are made from the dal, rice and milk of past meals. The meal does not end at your mouth. It becomes part of you.

teachings.teaching: This old Ayurvedic text teaches six tastes, sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent, and says that a good meal brings all of them in a fitting way.
teachings.link: The Ugadi pachadi is this teaching in a bowl. Science lists five tastes instead of six, but both ways of sorting ask the cook to look for balance, and not to let one taste be the boss.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Miracle of Mindfulness (1975), the tangerine
teachings.teaching: The Buddhist teacher Thich Nhat Hanh asks us to eat a tangerine slowly, giving it our whole attention. He says that if our mind is somewhere else, we are not really eating the tangerine.
teachings.link: The tongue test is a way of paying attention to taste. When you slow down, you notice more than the one word 'sweet'. You notice the first taste, how it changes, and what comes next.

science.text: Taste cells for sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami each use their own kind of sensor. Scientists have been finding these sensors for about twenty-five years. A child's tongue has them all over.
Whether fat is a sixth basic taste, and whether the body senses other things in food that we do not call tastes, is still argued.

other_view.view: They say that tastes are pleasant to talk about, but a body needs nutrients, and nutrients are measured, not tasted. A meal with all six rasas is not proof that it is balanced. Traditional meals, however much they are loved, should still be checked against what children actually need.

practice.title: One slow taste
practice.say: Take a very small piece of jaggery or one raisin. Put it on your tongue and do not chew. Close your eyes. Notice the first taste. Then move it to the side of your tongue, then the back. Notice if the taste changes. Breathe slowly through your nose. Then chew very slowly and notice what comes next.
practice.kid: Put a tiny piece of jaggery on your tongue. Close your eyes. Do not chew. Move it around. What do you taste now?

ask: Is sweet a thing in the sugar, or a thing that happens when sugar meets a tongue?
When you eat, where does the food stop and you begin?
If a taste is a message, who sent it, and who is it for?
roots.art: A girl with her eyes closed holding a piece of jaggery on her tongue, with fine lines running from the jaggery to a sugarcane field, a farmer, the sun and back to her.

how_we_found_out.story: For about a hundred years, children were shown a map of the tongue. Sweet was at the tip, sour and salty were at the sides, and bitter was at the back. The map began in 1901, when a German scientist named David Hänig tested how strongly people sensed tastes on different parts of the tongue. He found only small differences. In 1942 the American psychologist Edwin Boring drew those numbers as a chart, and textbooks turned the chart into a map where each taste had its own zone. Nobody checked it for decades. In 1974 Virginia Collings, a scientist in the USA, tested people carefully. Every taste could be sensed in every part of the tongue that has taste buds, and the differences were small. Later scientists found the sensors for each taste on cells all over the tongue.
how_we_found_out.who: David Hänig (1901), Edwin Boring (1942) and Virginia Collings (1974)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed that each taste is sensed only in its own zone on the tongue. A chart of small differences in how sensitive each part is had been turned into a map of separate zones. Collings tested people part by part and found that every taste is sensed everywhere.

experiments.title: The Blind Taste Test: does each taste have its own place on the tongue?
experiments.question: Is sweet sensed only at the tip, and bitter only at the back? Or can every part of the tongue sense every taste?
experiments.predict: Before you start, draw a tongue and mark where you think each taste is strongest: sweet, salty, sour and bitter. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Every touch uses the same amount of liquid on a new cotton bud, for the same 2 seconds, with the tongue dried first. The tester has their eyes shut and does not know which cup is which. Only two things change: the taste and the part of the tongue. Plain water is the control. It checks whether the tester is really tasting or only guessing. The order of the touches is shuffled, so that no taste is always tested first or last.
results_table: Tip: taste said and strength (0 to 3)
Left edge: taste said and strength (0 to 3)
Right edge: taste said and strength (0 to 3)
Back: taste said and strength (0 to 3)

materials.item: 5 small steel katoris or cups, with a number written on the bottom of each
20 clean, new cotton buds (one for each touch; a pack costs about Rs 20), or 20 small twists of clean tissue. With 2 or more testers, count 20 for each tester.
1 teaspoon of sugar, a quarter teaspoon of salt, and 1 teaspoon of lemon juice
a small piece of raw karela (bitter gourd) as big as your thumb, or half a teaspoon of methi seeds soaked in 3 tablespoons of water the night before (8 hours)
about 15 tablespoons of clean water in a tumbler, plus a second tumbler for rinsing
a tablespoon, a teaspoon, a grater and a clean cloth for squeezing the karela
a bowl for spitting, a tissue to dry the tongue, paper, a pencil, coloured pencils and the results table

experiments.safety: Every tester gets their own new buds and never shares a bud. Everything in the cups is ordinary food in tiny amounts. Do not test anyone who is allergic to lemon, karela or methi. A grown-up grates the karela. Use only drops of karela juice, and use a new bud for every touch. Never put a used bud back in a cup, and do not let the child bite the bud. Touch the back of the tongue gently, and stop at once if the child coughs or gags.
experiments.record: Write the taste that was said and the strength from 0 to 3 for every touch. Then colour a drawing of the tongue to show where each taste was named correctly.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you test the tongue map from old books. You touch tiny drops of four tastes to different parts of the tongue, with the tester's eyes shut.

setup.art: Five numbered katoris in a row: sugar water, salt water, lemon water, karela water and plain water, with a folded paper key beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Make five cups. Number them and keep the key hidden.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut and tongue out, while a parent dabs a drop of liquid from a cotton bud on the tip of the child's tongue.
setup.caption: 2. The child shuts their eyes. The parent touches a damp bud to one part of the tongue.

setup.art: A drawing of a tongue seen from above, with four marked zones: tip, left edge, right edge and back, and a small grid of tick marks.
setup.caption: 3. The child says the taste and its strength. The parent writes it in the table.

setup.art: A child rinsing her mouth with water and spitting into a bowl, next to a clock showing 20 seconds.
setup.caption: 4. Rinse and wait 20 seconds. Then do the next touch.

flow.do: Draw a large tongue on paper. Ask your child to mark where they think sweet, salty, sour and bitter are strongest. Ask why. Write the guess down. Do not correct it.
flow.say: Here is a tongue. Where do you think sweet is strongest? Where is bitter strongest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw a tongue. Mark where each taste is strongest. Say why you think so.

ask.q: Why do you think that taste is strongest there?
good: My teacher showed a map like that.
I think the tip tastes sweet things first.
I am not sure, I am guessing.

flow.parent: Many children have seen the old tongue map in a book, and will draw it. That is fine. Write down exactly what they say, and do not say yet that the map is wrong. If your child does not know, ask them to guess anyway.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Blind Taste Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up makes the cups while the child looks away. Cup 1: 1 teaspoon of sugar in 3 tablespoons of water. Cup 2: a quarter teaspoon of salt in 3 tablespoons of water. Cup 3: 1 teaspoon of lemon juice in 3 tablespoons of water. Cup 4: karela juice. Cup 5: plain water.
flow.say: I will make five cups while you look away. One is sweet, one is salty, one is sour, one is bitter, and one is only water.
flow.kid: Look away while a grown-up makes five cups. One of them is only water.
flow.parent: For the bitter cup, grate a piece of karela as big as your thumb, squeeze it through a clean cloth, and mix 1 teaspoon of the juice into 3 tablespoons of water. No karela? Soak half a teaspoon of methi seeds in 3 tablespoons of water for 8 hours, and use that water. Taste a drop of each cup yourself first. A cup that has almost no taste needs more sugar, salt, lemon or karela. A cup that is harsh needs more water. The cups are the same for every tester. Write the key on a paper and fold it: 1 sweet, 2 salty, 3 sour, 4 bitter, 5 water. Keep it hidden.

check.q: Why is there a cup of plain water among the tastes?
options: To check whether the tester is really tasting, or only guessing
To make the other cups weaker
To give the tester something to drink
check.why: If the tester names a taste for plain water, the test shows they are guessing, and a taste they name for other cups may be a guess too. Plain water is a control: the thing that should give no taste.

flow.context: In this step, a grown-up makes the five cups. Each one has a different taste, and one is only water.

flow.do: Rinse the child's mouth with water. Ask them to sit with eyes shut and tongue out. Dry the tongue with a tissue. Touch the tip of the tongue once with a damp bud, so the child knows what is coming.
flow.say: Shut your eyes and stick out your tongue. I will dry it first. Then I will touch it with a damp bud for two seconds.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Stick out your tongue. A grown-up will dry it and touch it with a bud.
flow.parent: Touch the bud to the rim of the cup after dipping it, so it is damp and not dripping. A dripping bud spreads the liquid over the whole tongue, and spoils the test. Practise once with a bud dipped in plain water.
flow.context: In this step, you practise how to touch the tongue before the real test begins.

flow.do: Do 20 touches in the order on your list. Dip a new bud into the cup. Touch the bud to the named part of the tongue for 2 seconds. Ask what the taste is. Write down the taste and its strength from 0 to 3. Rinse and wait 20 seconds.
flow.say: Tell me what you taste, and how strong it is, from nothing to very strong. Rinse your mouth. Wait twenty seconds. Then we do the next one.
flow.kid: Say what you taste. Say how strong it is, from 0 to 3. Then rinse.

ask.q: What do you notice when the taste is on the back of your tongue?
good: It is the same taste as at the tip.
It was a bit weaker.
It was stronger than I thought.

flow.parent: Here is the order of the 20 touches. Each one gives the cup, then the part of the tongue. 1: sweet, back. 2: sour, tip. 3: water, left edge. 4: salty, right edge. 5: sweet, left edge. 6: water, back. 7: sour, right edge. 8: salty, tip. 9: water, right edge. 10: sweet, tip. 11: salty, left edge. 12: sour, back. 13: water, tip. 14: bitter, left edge. 15: salty, back. 16: sour, left edge. 17: sweet, right edge. 18: bitter, right edge. 19: bitter, back. 20: bitter, tip. With 2 to 4 children, give each child a job and swap after each tester: tester (eyes shut), toucher (dips and touches), recorder (writes the table), and timer or rinse-helper. Every child can do the whole list in turn, which takes about 15 minutes each. If time is short, split the list: the first tester does touches 1 to 7, the next 8 to 14, the next 15 to 20, and you pool all the dots on one tongue drawing. One child alone with a parent works as written. Bitter comes mostly at the end on purpose, because it lingers and would spoil the other tastes. Your child may start to guess bitter near the end. Note it if they do. Use a new bud every time. The left edge and right edge are about halfway back along the side. For the back, touch the middle of the tongue as far back as is comfortable. Some answers may be wrong, or the strength may be 0. That is a result. Write what you hear.

check.q: Your child says 'sweet' for a touch of plain water. What does that mean for the test?
options: Sometimes the tester guesses, so the other answers need careful reading
The test has failed and must be thrown away
The water must have been sweet
check.why: People sometimes name a taste they expect. The water cup shows how often that happens, so you can read the other answers more carefully. It is a normal and useful result.

flow.context: In this step, you do the 20 touches. A new bud is used for each touch, and the tester's eyes stay shut.

flow.do: Draw a tongue with four zones. For each taste, put a coloured dot in every zone where it was named correctly. Count the dots. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why. Then compare with their first guess.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you find? Why do you think it came out that way?
flow.kid: Colour a dot where each taste was named right. Say what you thought, what you found, and why.
flow.think: Look at your first drawing. Which part did the test show to be wrong?
flow.parent: Most children find that every taste was named correctly in most zones, though some were stronger than others. If nothing is tasted at the back, check that the bud was wet enough, and try again with a bit more liquid on the bud. The tip and the edges are often a little stronger than the middle, because they tend to have more taste buds. The back is often strongest for bitter. These differences are small and vary from person to person. If the dots do not look like that, say so. Messy results are real results. Wet buds, nerves and guessing can all spoil a result. After your child has said what they found, you can explain: taste buds for every taste are spread across the tongue. The old map came from a mistake in the 1940s. The card on the tongue map tells the whole story.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Blind Taste Test. You mark your results on a tongue and say what they show.

experiments.title: Wake Up the Moong: what do soaking and sprouting change in a seed?
experiments.question: Does a moong seed that has been soaked, or soaked and sprouted, cook faster than a dry one? And how much heavier do the seeds get?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which will cook softest first: dry moong, soaked moong or sprouted moong? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three batches start as 50 grams of the same moong. Twelve seeds from each batch are counted out and tied loosely in a small cloth bag, with a different colour of string for each batch. All three bags cook together in the same big pan of gently boiling water, so the heat is exactly the same. Only the preparation differs: dry, soaked, or soaked and sprouted. The dry batch is the control. Each bag is tested for softness the same way, by pressing one cooled seed between thumb and finger.

materials.item: 150 grams of whole green moong (fresh stock, from a shop that sells a lot of dal), in three equal portions of 50 grams (about 4 level tablespoons each). Old moong may not sprout.
a kitchen scale that shows grams, or a measuring cup or tumbler if you have no scale. Your kirana shop can also weigh the seeds for you.
3 bowls (A, B and C), and 1 sieve or small colander for sprouting
a clean, damp cloth to cover the sprouting moong
water: 450 millilitres for soaking, and 1 big pan with about 1 litre of water for cooking
3 squares of old thin cotton cloth or muslin (about 15 centimetres across) and 3 strings or rubber bands, each a different colour, to make 3 small bags
a long spoon, a plate, a ruler marked in millimetres, a timer and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the cooking, because the pan, the boiling water and the steam are hot. A grown-up lifts the bags out with a long spoon. Children stand back from the stove. They press a seed, on a plate or between thumb and finger, only after the seed has cooled for a minute. Do not eat raw sprouts if anyone at home is very young, old or ill. Wash sprouts well and cook them. This test cooks them well, so it is safe to taste at the end. Skip tasting if anyone has a pulse allergy.
experiments.record: Write the weights, the tail length and the cooking times in the table. Draw the three kinds of seed: dry, soaked and sprouted. Then write what you thought, what you saw and why.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you wake up moong seeds by soaking and sprouting them. Then you cook all three batches together and time how long each takes to turn soft.

setup.art: Three small bowls labelled A dry, B soaked and C sprouted, each with 50 grams of moong, and a kitchen scale on the table.
setup.caption: 1. Weigh three equal portions of moong. Soak B and C in water overnight. Leave A dry.

setup.art: Swollen soaked moong being drained in a sieve, with a damp cloth laid over the sieve, in a warm dark corner.
setup.caption: 2. Next morning, drain B and C. Cover C with a damp cloth to sprout.

setup.art: A child measuring a small white sprout on a moong seed with a ruler, next to a scale showing a heavier weight.
setup.caption: 3. On day 3, weigh each batch and measure the tails.

setup.art: One big pan on a stove with three small cloth bags tied with red, blue and green strings, and a grown-up lifting one bag on a long spoon onto a plate to cool.
setup.caption: 4. Cook the three bags together in one pan. Every 5 minutes, test one seed from each bag.

schedule.what: Guess which moong will cook fastest. Weigh three portions of moong. In the evening, put bowls B and C to soak in water.
In the morning, drain B and C for 2 minutes, then weigh them. Put B in fresh water in the fridge. Cover C with a damp cloth and let it sprout. Rinse C twice, morning and evening.
Weigh and measure all three. Cook 12 seeds of each in three bags in one pan and test every 5 minutes. Write what you found.

flow.do: Weigh three portions of 50 grams of moong, or measure 4 level tablespoons each. Put them in bowls A, B and C. Pour 150 millilitres of water on B and on C. Leave A dry. Write the weights.
flow.say: We will soak two bowls of moong to wake the seeds up, and leave one bowl dry. Which will cook fastest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put equal moong in three bowls. Add water to B and C. Leave A dry.

ask.q: What do you think the moong in water will do overnight?
good: The seeds will get bigger.
They will soak up the water.
They might start to grow.

flow.parent: Do this in the evening. The soaking takes 8 to 10 hours. With 2 or 3 children, each child looks after one bowl (A, B or C), and weighs and records it. With 4 children, the fourth child is the timer and writer. One child alone looks after all three bowls. Write the guesses on the table. If you have no scale, write the volume of the seeds in a measuring cup instead.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wake Up the Moong. You weigh the seeds and start soaking two bowls.

flow.do: In the morning, drain B and C in a sieve for 2 minutes and shake off the extra water. Weigh each one and write the weights. Put B back in clean water in the fridge. Put C in a sieve, cover it with a damp cloth, and keep it in a warm, dark place. Rinse C twice a day.
flow.say: The seeds have soaked all night. Let us weigh them. Bowl B goes to the fridge in water. Bowl C goes in the sieve, to grow.
flow.kid: Drain B and C. Weigh them. B goes in the fridge. C goes in the sieve under a damp cloth.
flow.wait: Leave C to sprout for about a day, rinsing the seeds in the morning and evening.
flow.parent: In a warm kitchen, tiny white tails show by the next morning. In cool weather, sprouting can take two days. In hot weather, rinse C three times a day, because sprouts can turn sour in the heat. If C is not sprouting, keep it warm and give it another day. If there is still no tail, the moong is too old. That is a result: write it down, and compare only A and B. Do not let the seeds sit in water, or they will go sour. If sprouts smell bad or feel slimy, throw them away.

check.q: The soaked moong weighs more than the dry moong. Where did the extra weight come from?
options: Water that the seeds soaked up
Food that the seeds made from nothing
Dirt from the bowl
check.why: A dry seed has very little water. Seeds soak up water through their skin and swell. The extra weight is water, so the soaked seeds weigh more.

flow.context: In this step, you drain and weigh the soaked seeds, and set one batch to sprout.

flow.do: On day 3, look at C. Measure the longest tail with a ruler in millimetres. Weigh A, B and C and write the weights. Count out 12 seeds from each bowl for the cooking test. Put the pan of water on to boil now. Draw one dry, one soaked and one sprouted seed.
flow.say: Look closely at the three kinds of seed. What is different? How long is the tail on the sprouted ones?
flow.kid: Look at A, B and C. Measure a tail on C. Draw one seed of each kind.

ask.q: What is the white tail on the sprouted moong?
good: It is a root.
It is the start of a new plant.
The seed has woken up.

flow.parent: The weights will not be exact. Soaked moong often weighs roughly double the dry moong, but yours may differ. A tail is the first root, and a good length is a few millimetres to a centimetre. If your sprouts are very short, write that down. The seeds are alive, and have started to grow.
flow.context: In this step, you look at what soaking and sprouting have done to the seeds.

flow.do: A grown-up puts 12 seeds of each batch into its own cloth bag. The bag is tied loosely, so the seeds can swell. All three bags go into the gently boiling pan at the same moment. Start the timer. Every 5 minutes, lift each bag with the long spoon, take out one seed, and put the bag back. Let the seed cool on the plate for a minute, and press it between thumb and finger. Soft means the seed squashes with no hard middle. Keep the water covering the bags, and top up with hot water.
flow.say: All three bags go in together. Every five minutes, I lift one seed from each bag. When it squashes with no hard middle, we write down the time.
flow.kid: Cook A, B and C together in one pan. Every 5 minutes, press one seed from each bag. Write the time when it is soft.

ask.q: Which bag will be soft first? How can you tell?
good: The sprouted one, because it is already awake.
The seeds that soaked are softer to start.
I will press one and see.

flow.parent: Stop at 40 minutes. If the dry moong is still hard at 40 minutes, write 40 plus. That is a result. Typical times for whole moong are about 10 minutes for sprouted, about 15 to 20 for soaked, and 35 to 45 or more for dry. The time for each batch depends on your moong and your flame, so your numbers may differ from anyone else's. All three bags share one pan, so the heat is the same. With 2 to 4 children, one reads the timer, one presses the cooled seeds and calls out soft or hard, and one writes. Swap after each round. The grown-up still lifts the bags. You can read the card on old ways of preparing food while you wait.

check.q: The sprouted moong turned soft in 10 minutes, and the dry moong needed more than 30. What does this suggest?
options: The water in the seed and the start of growth made the seed softer to cook
The sprouted bag sat in hotter water
The dry moong is a different seed
check.why: All three bags sat in the same boiling water. Only the preparation changed. A seed that has taken in water and begun to grow has already started to soften inside, so the seed cooks faster.

flow.context: In this step, you cook all three batches in one pan and time how long each takes to turn soft.

flow.do: Look at the table. Compare the weights and the cooking times. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why. Taste a little of each cooked batch if your child wants to.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you find? Why do you think it came out that way?
flow.kid: Look at your numbers. Say what you thought, what you found, and why.
flow.think: People soak dal before cooking, and sprout moong for salads. What might they have noticed?
flow.parent: Most families find that the dry moong takes much the longest, the soaked moong is quicker, and the sprouted moong quickest of all. If your numbers do not follow this, say so. After your child has said what they found, explain: soaking lets water in and starts the seed waking up. Sprouting goes further. The seed makes enzymes that break down some of the stored food, and makes a little vitamin C, which dry seeds do not have. The card on old ways of preparing food says more.
flow.context: This is the last step of Wake Up the Moong. You compare your numbers and say what they show.

games.title: Feast Builder: fill your mat with dishes from all over India
games.context: This is a card game. You draw dishes from different parts of India and build a feast on your mat. A good feast has every food job and all six tastes.

setup.art: Twenty-four dish cards in a face-down pile in the middle of a table, with a feast mat and a pencil in front of each of three players.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the mat. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: A girl reading the front of a card that shows the Ugadi pachadi, while she holds up one finger for energy and two fingers for taste.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a card. Read only the front. Guess one job and one taste.

setup.art: The same card turned over to show its jobs and tastes, with the girl placing it in the protective box of her mat and colouring two taste circles.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Score your guesses. Place the card on your mat and colour its tastes.

printables.title: 24 two-sided dish cards: a dish and where it is from on the front, its jobs and tastes on the back

items.f: Idli with sambar, from Tamil Nadu. Idli is steamed from a batter of rice and urad dal. Sambar is made of toor dal, vegetables and tamarind.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the rice, body-building from the dals, protective from the vegetables. Tastes: sour from the tamarind, pungent from the chilli, and salty. The batter is fermented by microbes.

items.f: Venn pongal, from Tamil Nadu. Rice and moong dal are cooked soft with ghee, black pepper and cumin.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the rice and ghee, body-building from the moong dal. Tastes: pungent from the pepper, and salty.

items.f: Sakkarai pongal, from Tamil Nadu. Rice and moong dal are cooked with jaggery, ghee, cardamom and cashew nuts.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the rice, jaggery and ghee, body-building from the moong dal and cashew. Taste: sweet. It is a festival dish, rich in sugar and ghee, so it suits special days.

items.f: Ragi mudde with saaru, from Karnataka. A ball of ragi flour is eaten with a thin dal soup that has tamarind and pepper.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the ragi, body-building from the dal. Ragi also has a lot of calcium. Tastes: sour from the tamarind, and pungent from the pepper.

items.f: Avial, from Kerala. Many vegetables are cooked with grated coconut, curd and curry leaves.
items.b: Jobs: protective from the vegetables, energy from the coconut. Tastes: sour from the curd, and salty. It is a part of the Onam sadya.

items.f: Pavakka thoran, from Kerala. Thin slices of karela are stir-fried with grated coconut.
items.b: Jobs: protective from the karela, energy from the coconut. Tastes: bitter from the karela, and salty.

items.f: Parippu with ghee, from Kerala. Cooked dal is mashed with a spoon of ghee. It is the first dish served with rice in a sadya.
items.b: Jobs: body-building from the dal, energy from the ghee. Taste: salty.

items.f: Payasam, from Kerala. Rice or ada is cooked in milk with jaggery or sugar.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the rice and sugar, body-building from the milk. Taste: sweet. It ends many festival meals.

items.f: Inji puli, from Kerala. Ginger, tamarind, green chilli and jaggery are cooked down to a thick sauce.
items.b: Jobs: protective, but only a little. A spoonful is eaten for the taste. Tastes: sweet from the jaggery, sour from the tamarind, and pungent from the ginger and chilli.

items.f: Ugadi pachadi, from Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Jaggery, tamarind, salt, neem flowers, pepper and raw mango pieces are mixed in one bowl.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the jaggery, protective from the raw mango. Tastes: all six. Sweet from the jaggery, sour from the tamarind, salty from the salt, bitter from the neem, pungent from the pepper, and astringent from the raw mango.

items.f: Dal baati churma, from Rajasthan. Baked wheat balls are broken into hot dal with ghee. Sweet churma is eaten beside it.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the wheat, ghee and churma, body-building from the dal. Tastes: sweet from the churma, and salty.

items.f: Bajra rotla with ghee and jaggery, from Gujarat. A thick flat bread of pearl millet is eaten with a spoon of ghee and a piece of jaggery.
items.b: Job: energy from the bajra, ghee and jaggery. Bajra is a millet, with fibre and iron. Taste: sweet.

items.f: Kadhi, from Gujarat. Buttermilk or curd is cooked with gram flour into a smooth, thin curry.
items.b: Job: body-building from the curd and the gram flour. Tastes: sour, and a little sweet.

items.f: Sarson ka saag with makki di roti and butter, from Punjab. Cooked mustard greens are eaten with maize flat bread.
items.b: Jobs: protective from the greens, energy from the maize and butter. Tastes: salty, with a little bitter and pungent from the mustard greens.

items.f: Macher jhol with rice, from Bengal. A thin fish curry with potato and spices is eaten with rice.
items.b: Jobs: body-building from the fish, energy from the rice and potato. Tastes: pungent from the chilli and mustard, and salty.

items.f: Shukto, from Bengal. Vegetables with a little karela are cooked in a light milky sauce. It is often served first in a meal.
items.b: Job: protective from the vegetables. Taste: bitter from the karela, then a little sweet.

items.f: Mishti doi, from Bengal. Milk is thickened with sugar or jaggery, then set into curd in a clay pot.
items.b: Jobs: body-building from the milk, energy from the sugar. Tastes: sweet, and a little sour. Bacteria set the curd.

items.f: Til-gul laddu, from Maharashtra. Roasted sesame seeds are rolled with jaggery into balls. It is eaten at Makar Sankranti, in the cool months.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the jaggery and the oil in the sesame, body-building from the sesame, protective from the calcium and iron in the sesame. Taste: sweet.

items.f: Sabudana khichdi, from Maharashtra. Soaked sago pearls are cooked with peanuts, potato and cumin. It is eaten on fasting days.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the sago, which is almost all starch, and the potato, body-building from the peanuts. Tastes: salty, and pungent from the green chilli.

items.f: Eromba, from Manipur. Boiled vegetables are mashed with chilli and fermented fish.
items.b: Jobs: protective from the vegetables, body-building from the fish. Tastes: pungent from the chilli, and salty. The fish is a fermented food.

items.f: Til pitha, from Assam. A rice flour pancake is rolled around a filling of sesame and jaggery. It is eaten at Bihu.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the rice and jaggery, body-building from the sesame. Taste: sweet.

items.f: Sheer khurma, from North India and Hyderabad. Vermicelli, dates and nuts are cooked in milk. It is eaten at Eid.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the vermicelli and dates, body-building from the milk and nuts. Taste: sweet.

items.f: Biryani with raita, from Hyderabad. Rice is cooked with spices and meat, or with vegetables. Raita is curd with cucumber and onion.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the rice, body-building from the meat or beans and the curd, protective from the cucumber and onion. Tastes: pungent from the spices, salty, and sour from the curd.

items.f: Murukku, from Tamil Nadu. Rice flour and urad dal flour are pressed into spirals and fried in oil.
items.b: Jobs: energy from the oil and rice flour, body-building from the urad dal flour, in a small amount. Taste: salty. It keeps for weeks because it has almost no water.

printables.title: A feast mat for each player, to draw on a sheet of paper
items: Draw three big boxes in a row. Label them ENERGY, BODY-BUILDING and PROTECTIVE.
Under the boxes, draw six small circles in a row. Write one taste by each circle: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent.
At the bottom, write the word SCORE and leave a space for a number.

rules: Each player has a feast mat and a pencil. Put the dish cards in a pile, with the fronts facing up.
Take turns. On your turn, take the top card and read only the front.
Before you turn the card over, say one job the dish does and one taste it has.
Turn the card over. Score 1 point if your job is on the back. Score 1 point if your taste is on the back.
Place the card in one of the job boxes on your mat, in a job the dish does. Colour the circle for each taste on the back.
Play until each player has taken 6 cards. Then count the points on your mat. Score 1 point for each coloured taste circle. Score 3 points for each job box with 2 or more dishes.
Score 5 more points if all six taste circles are coloured. The player with the most points wins. If you tie, share the win.
Playing alone: take 12 cards, one after another, and try to colour all six circles. Beat your own score the next time.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards with blunt scissors. No printer? Copy the dish names onto 24 paper slips and let the parent read the back from the phone. Draw a feast mat for each player. Shuffle the cards into a pile with the dish names facing up. Give each player a pencil.
flow.say: Today we will build a feast. Each dish gives energy, or builds the body, or protects it. Each dish also has tastes. Let us see how many we can fill.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Draw your feast mat. Shuffle the cards.
flow.parent: The game works for 1 to 4 players, and 24 cards give each of 4 players 6 cards. Some cards have fish or meat. Take out any card your family does not eat, and count the cards on the mats at the end. The three jobs are the ones from Class 3. Energy foods are mostly grains, sugar and fats. Body-building foods are pulses, milk, eggs, fish, meat and nuts. Protective foods are vegetables and fruits. Remind your child of the three jobs, and explain the six tastes of shad rasa.
flow.context: This is the first step of Feast Builder. You make the mat and set up the cards.

flow.do: Play the first round. Each player takes a card, reads the front, and guesses one job and one taste. Then they turn the card over, score, and place it on the mat.
flow.say: Read the front and look at the foods. Which job does this dish do? Which taste does it have? Say it before you turn the card.
flow.kid: Read the front. Guess a job and a taste. Then turn the card.

ask.q: How did you guess the job from the front of the card?
good: I looked at what the dish is made of.
Rice and ghee are energy.
Dal and milk build the body.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first round of cards and learn how the scoring works.

flow.do: Play the next rounds until every player has 6 cards on the mat. Ask the question below after the third card.
flow.say: Is there a job box on your mat that is still empty? Which taste circles are still white? Which dish could fill them?
flow.kid: Look at your mat. Which job is empty? Which tastes are missing?

ask.q: Which card would you like to draw next, to fill your mat?
good: One with a bitter taste.
A protective dish, because I have mostly energy.
A dish with an astringent taste.

check.q: A player has mostly energy dishes on her mat. What kind of dish should she hope to draw?
options: A body-building or protective dish, to fill the empty boxes
Another energy dish, since they score the most
A dish she likes, whatever it does
check.why: A balanced meal has all three jobs. If a job box is empty, the meal is missing something, so the player needs a dish from that group.

flow.context: In this step, you play the rest of the cards and look at what your mat is missing.

flow.do: Count each mat. Score 1 point for each coloured taste circle. Score 3 points for each job box with 2 or more dishes. Add 5 points for all six tastes. Add up the total.
flow.say: Let us count each mat. One point for every coloured circle. Three points for every box with two or more dishes. Five points if all six tastes are there.
flow.kid: Count your coloured circles. Add 3 for each box with 2 or more dishes. Add 5 for all six tastes.
flow.context: In this step, you count your points and see who has built the best feast.

flow.do: Look at the winning mat. Which tastes were easy to fill, and which were hard? Which taste could only the Ugadi pachadi fill? Ask your child what a real feast would need.
flow.say: Which taste was hardest to fill? Which dish gave the most tastes at once? What would your own festival feast need?
flow.kid: Which taste was hardest? Which dish had the most tastes?
flow.think: Why might the people who made the Ugadi pachadi have put all six tastes in one bowl?
flow.parent: Bitter and astringent are the hardest tastes to fill. Few dishes have them, and many families eat little of them. The Ugadi pachadi, shukto and pavakka thoran are the bitter dishes. A good answer to the think question: the pachadi is a way of tasting every kind of taste, once, on the first day of the year.
flow.context: This is the last step of Feast Builder. You talk about which tastes were hard to find.

activities.title: Six Tastes in One Bowl: make a mini pachadi

materials.item: a small piece of jaggery, as big as a thumb tip
a lump of tamarind the size of a marble, soaked in 3 tablespoons of warm water
a pinch of salt
a few drops of karela juice, or a spoon of methi seeds soaked in water for 8 hours, or 2 or 3 clean neem flowers if you have them
a pinch of black pepper, or a tiny piece of green chilli
a piece of raw mango, raw banana or amla as big as a thumb tip (or a spoon of cold, strong black tea with no sugar, which is easy to find all year)
a bowl, 6 teaspoons for each child (never share a spoon), a tumbler of plain water and paper for scoring

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the raw mango and the chilli. Keep chilli away from eyes. Use a tiny amount, and skip it if your child does not want it. Use ground pepper, not whole peppercorns, which can be a choking risk. With 2 to 4 children, each child tastes from their own spoons. Skip any ingredient that anyone is allergic to. Only use neem flowers that are clean and fresh, and only 2 or 3 of them.
activities.record: Write each taste and its strength from 0 to 3. Then write the strength of the mixed pachadi, and which taste is the strongest in it.
activities.context: In this activity, you taste six ingredients one by one, and then mix them into a small pachadi. You find out what it takes to keep six tastes in balance.

setup.art: Six teaspoons in a row, each holding one ingredient: jaggery, tamarind pulp, salt, karela juice, pepper and raw mango.
setup.caption: 1. Put each ingredient on its own spoon, with its name beside it.

setup.art: A child with eyes closed tasting one spoon, while another person holds up three fingers beside a paper score sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Taste each one alone. Give it a score from 0 to 3.

setup.art: All six ingredients mixed in a steel bowl with a spoon, and a child tasting a small spoonful with a thoughtful face.
setup.caption: 3. Mix them in a little at a time. Taste the mix, and fix the boss taste.

flow.do: Lay out the six ingredients, each in a separate spoon, with its name beside it. Ask your child which taste each one will have, and which they think will be the strongest.
flow.say: Here are six ingredients. Which taste will each one have? Which do you think is the strongest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the six spoons. Guess the taste of each one. Which is strongest?

ask.q: Which ingredient do you think will taste the strongest, and why?
good: The bitter one, because bitter is always strong.
The chilli, because it burns.
The jaggery, because it is very sweet.

flow.context: This is the first step of Six Tastes in One Bowl. You guess before you taste.

flow.do: Taste the ingredients one by one. Rinse your mouth with water between each. After each, say the taste and score it from 0 to 3. Write the scores on the paper.
flow.say: Taste one spoon. Say what the taste is, and how strong it is, from nothing to very strong. Rinse your mouth, and then do the next one.
flow.kid: Taste one spoon. Say the taste and score it from 0 to 3. Rinse.

ask.q: Which one did you not expect?
good: The pepper felt hot, not like a taste.
The raw mango made my mouth dry.
The karela was more bitter than I expected.

flow.parent: Pepper and chilli give a burning feeling and not a taste. Raw mango, raw banana and amla give a dry, puckering feeling. These are the pungent and astringent of shad rasa. Science says they are feelings of heat and touch. Taste the bitter one last, because it lingers.
flow.context: In this step, you taste each ingredient alone and give it a score.

flow.do: Mix the jaggery, the tamarind water, the salt and a small piece of raw mango in the bowl. Add the bitter ingredient, then the pepper, a little at a time. Taste after each addition. Aim for every taste to score about 2.
flow.say: Put the ingredients in a bowl, a little at a time. Taste after each one. Which taste is the boss now? What does the bowl need?
flow.kid: Mix a little of each. Taste. Which taste is the boss? Fix it.

check.q: Your pachadi tastes mostly of tamarind. What should you do to balance it?
options: Add a little more of the other tastes, and not more tamarind
Add more tamarind to make it stronger
Throw it away and start again with only jaggery
check.why: A balanced pachadi has no boss taste. If sour is the boss, the other five tastes need a little more, or the sour needs to be thinned with water.

flow.context: In this step, you mix the six ingredients and balance the tastes.
flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, give each child their own six spoons and score sheet. Each child writes their own 0 to 3 scores, and then you compare: do all of you give the same score to the same taste? Different scores are a real result, because tongues differ. The group then mixes one pachadi together, with one child adding each ingredient.

flow.do: Taste the finished pachadi from the tip, the side and the back of the tongue. Ask your child to say whether any taste is missing, and why a festival might begin with this dish.
