flow.say: Taste from the tip of your tongue, then the side, then the back. Can you find all six? Why do you think a festival begins with this?
flow.kid: Taste the pachadi. Can you find all six? Why start a year with it?
flow.think: Many families say the six tastes stand for the different feelings of the year to come. What do you think?
flow.parent: Tradition says the pachadi reminds us that a year holds joy, sadness, anger and surprise, and that we should take all of it. There is no single right answer. If the pachadi is hard to eat, a few spoonfuls is enough.
flow.context: In this step, you taste the finished bowl and think about why it is part of a festival.

activities.title: The Seven-Day Food Diary: which group goes missing?

materials.item: a sheet of paper ruled into a table: 7 days across and 4 rows down, for energy foods, body-building foods, protective foods and sweet or packet snacks
a pencil and coloured pencils
the food groups card from Feast Builder, or the group list on the diary sheet

schedule.what: Draw the table. Write down yesterday's food as a practice. Learn which row each food goes in.
In the evening, mark each food you ate today in its row.
In the evening, mark each food you ate today in its row.
In the evening, mark each food you ate today in its row.
In the evening, mark each food you ate today in its row.
In the evening, mark each food you ate today in its row.
Mark today's foods. Count each row. Draw a pictograph and say which group goes missing.

activities.record: Make a mark for every dish you ate, in its row, each day. At the end, draw a pictograph with one picture standing for 2 marks.
activities.context: In this activity, you keep a diary of everything you eat for seven days. You sort it into groups, and find out which group is thin or missing.

setup.art: A paper table with seven day columns and four rows labelled energy, body-building, protective, and sweet or packet snacks, with a few marks in the first column.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the table. Each evening, mark what you ate that day.

setup.art: A girl at a table holding a pencil and looking at a plate of idli, sambar and a glass of milk, with marks going into three rows.
setup.caption: 2. Put each dish in its row. A dish can go in more than one row.

setup.art: A pictograph with four rows and little pictures, one standing for 2 marks, with the shortest row circled.
setup.caption: 3. On day 7, count each row and draw the pictograph.

flow.do: Draw the table with 7 columns and 4 rows. Talk through yesterday's food and mark it in a practice column. Check each dish goes in the right row. A dish can go in more than one row.
flow.say: Let us practise with yesterday. What did you eat? Which job does it do? A dish can do more than one job, so it can go in more than one row.
flow.kid: Draw the table. Mark what you ate yesterday. Which row does each dish go in?

ask.q: Which row do you think will be fullest this week, and which emptiest?
good: Energy will be fullest, because we eat rice and roti every day.
Protective will be emptiest, because I do not like vegetables.
I am not sure, I will find out.

flow.parent: Rows: energy (rice, roti, ragi, potato, sugar, oil, ghee), body-building (dal, milk, curd, eggs, fish, meat, paneer, nuts), protective (vegetables and fruit), and sweet or packet snacks (chips, biscuits, fizzy drinks, sweets). Do not judge what your child eats. The diary is there to find out, not to judge.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Seven-Day Food Diary. You draw the table and practise with yesterday.

flow.do: Each evening, ask your child to list what they ate that day. Make one mark in the right row for every dish. Do not change what you eat for the diary.
flow.say: What did you eat today? Let us put each dish in its row.
flow.kid: Write down what you ate today. Mark a row for each dish.
flow.parent: Repeat this each evening for days 2 to 6. If your child forgets a meal, ask what they had at school or at a friend's home. A snack counts. Do not change meals to make a better diary. With 2 to 4 children, each child keeps their own diary, because school lunches and snacks differ. Compare the pictographs on day 7.
flow.context: In this step, you mark one day of food in your table. You repeat it each evening.

flow.do: On day 7, mark today's food. Count the marks in each row. Draw a pictograph with one picture for every 2 marks. Mark the shortest row with a circle.
flow.say: Let us count each row. One picture stands for two marks. Which row is longest? Which is shortest?
flow.kid: Count each row. Draw one picture for every 2 marks.

ask.q: What does your pictograph show? Is any row empty or very short?
good: The protective row is the shortest.
We eat a lot of energy foods.
The snack row is bigger than I thought.

check.q: A diary shows many energy foods and very few protective foods. What should the family do?
options: Add more vegetables and fruits over the next week, without blaming anyone
Stop eating energy foods completely
Do nothing, since the body will balance itself
check.why: A short row shows what the week is missing. The answer is to add some of that group in ways the family enjoys. Energy foods are still needed, so there is no reason to stop them.

flow.context: In this step, you count your marks and draw a pictograph of the week.

flow.do: Look at the pictograph together. Ask your child to pick one change for next week, such as adding a fruit or a green vegetable. Write it at the bottom of the page.
flow.say: Which group was thin this week? What is one small thing we could add next week? We will try it and see.
flow.kid: Which row is short? Pick one thing to add next week.
flow.think: Is a thin row a mistake, or just a fact about this week?
flow.parent: Keep this positive. A thin row is information, not a failure. One change is enough. If the snack row is long, notice it without criticism, and ask what could be added beside it.
flow.context: In this step, you pick one small change for next week.

activities.title: Why This Food, Now? A festival food calendar

materials.item: a large sheet of paper and coloured pencils
the festival list in the steps below
a grandparent, aunt, neighbour or friend to ask, in person or by phone

activities.record: Draw a year wheel with 12 months. Put each festival food in its month, with a label for its season and the food group it belongs to.
activities.context: In this activity, you find out when festival foods are made, and why. You place them on a wheel of the year and look for patterns.

setup.art: A big circle divided into twelve months, with five festival foods drawn in the right places around it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a year wheel. Put each festival food in its month.

setup.art: A girl on a phone call with her grandmother, with a notebook open and a pencil in her hand.
setup.caption: 2. Ask someone at home, or on the phone, about a festival food they make.

setup.art: The year wheel with small notes beside each food: a sugarcane stalk for Pongal, a mango for Ugadi, a sesame seed for Sankranti.
setup.caption: 3. For each food, write what grows in that season and which job it does.

flow.do: Draw a wheel of twelve months. Place six foods on it. Pongal sweet goes in January, and til-gul at Makar Sankranti goes in January too. Ugadi pachadi goes in March or April, and Bihu pitha in January (Magh Bihu) or April (Bohag Bihu). Onam sadya goes in August or September, and Diwali sweets in October or November.
flow.say: Here is a wheel of the year. Let us put six festival foods on it, each in the month where it belongs.
flow.kid: Draw a wheel with 12 months. Put six festival foods in their months.

ask.q: Which foods are close together on the wheel? Which are far apart?
good: Pongal and til-gul are both in January.
Diwali sweets are far from Ugadi.
There is a gap in the summer.

flow.parent: Festival dates change a little each year. Eid moves through the whole year, because it follows the moon. Pongal, Sankranti and Lohri fall in mid-January. Onam is in August or September. Diwali is in October or November.
flow.context: This is the first step of Why This Food, Now? You draw the wheel and place six festival foods.

flow.do: For each food, write what grows or is gathered in that season. For example, sugarcane and new rice in January, raw mango and neem flowers in spring, and fresh vegetables after the monsoon. Count how many foods use something from that very season. Write the count on the wheel.
flow.say: What is fresh in the market at that time of year? Pongal comes after the rice harvest. Ugadi comes when raw mango and neem flowers appear.
flow.kid: What grows in that season? Write it by each food.

check.q: Why might a sweet made of sesame and jaggery be a food of the cool months?
options: It is rich in fat and energy, and sesame and jaggery are gathered around then
It cools the body down in winter
It is only a custom with no link to the season
check.why: Sesame has a lot of oil, and jaggery is a quick fuel, so a laddu gives plenty of energy in cold weather. Sesame is also harvested around then. Festival foods often follow the season in this way.

flow.context: In this step, you link each food to its season and the crops around it.

flow.do: Ask a grown-up one question: what is made for one festival at home, and why? Write down what they say, and add the dish to your wheel with its food job.
flow.say: Ask someone: what is made at your home for one festival? Why is that dish made? Write down what they tell you.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up what they cook for a festival, and why. Write it down.
flow.think: Why do people cook special food on special days, and not the same food every day?
flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, each child asks a different person and adds their dish to the one shared wheel. Listen to the answer without correcting it. Families often have a reason that goes beyond nutrition: it is what a mother made, it keeps well, or it is shared with neighbours. These reasons are part of the answer. Add a dish from your own family's tradition to the wheel.
flow.context: In this step, you ask someone about a festival dish from your own family and add it to the wheel.

activities.title: Millet Hunt: find, cook and compare

materials.item: ragi flour, or another millet flour such as jowar or bajra, about 2 tablespoons (a small packet costs about Rs 30 to 50; if you cannot find any millet, use whole wheat atta instead and compare it with rice flour)
2 tablespoons of rice flour, or powdered rice
two small pans, 2 long spoons, a stove, a ruler and a grown-up to cook
a pinch of salt or a little jaggery for taste
the packet of ragi flour, to read the label

activities.safety: A grown-up works the stove. The porridge is hot and can spit when it bubbles, so stand back and use a long spoon. Let it cool for a few minutes before tasting.
activities.record: Write the colour, smell, thickness and taste of each porridge. Write one way the millet and rice are different.
activities.context: In this activity, you cook a thin porridge of a millet and a thin porridge of rice, and compare them. You also read what is written on a millet packet.

setup.art: A packet of ragi flour beside a packet of rice flour, with two small pans on a stove.
setup.caption: 1. Mix 1 tablespoon of each flour with half a cup of cold water in a pan.

setup.art: A grown-up stirring a thin brown porridge in one pan and a thin white porridge in another.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up stirs each pan on a low flame for 5 to 10 minutes, until it thickens and smells cooked.

setup.art: Two small bowls side by side, one dark brown and one white, with a child comparing them with a spoon.
setup.caption: 3. Let them cool. Look, smell, feel and taste. Compare.

flow.do: Read the label on the ragi packet. Find the name of the millet, how much fibre it has, and any other numbers. Then mix 1 tablespoon of ragi flour with half a cup of cold water in one pan. Do the same with rice flour in another. Guess which porridge will be thicker, and which will be darker.
flow.say: Let us read the packet first. What does it say about fibre? Now we make two porridges, one of ragi and one of rice.
flow.kid: Read the packet. Mix 1 spoon of flour with cold water in each pan.

ask.q: What do you think will be different between the two porridges?
good: The colour will be different.
The ragi will be thicker.
I think the ragi will taste stronger.

flow.parent: Ragi flour is dark brown, and rice flour is white. Mixing the flour with cold water first stops lumps. If you cannot find millet flour, ask a neighbour for a spoonful. Some labels give calcium, and some give only fibre.
flow.context: This is the first step of Millet Hunt. You read the packet and mix the flours.

flow.do: A grown-up cooks each pan on a low flame, stirring all the time, for 5 to 10 minutes. It should thicken and stop smelling raw. Ragi takes longer than rice. Add a pinch of salt or a little jaggery. Pour each into a bowl and let it cool for a few minutes.
flow.say: Stir slowly so it does not form lumps. It will thicken in about five minutes. Let it cool a little before we taste.
flow.kid: A grown-up cooks the porridge. Stir slowly. Wait for it to cool.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up cooks the two porridges for about five minutes.

flow.do: Look at each porridge, smell it, feel it with a spoon, and taste a small amount. Put one spoonful of each on a flat plate, wait 10 seconds, and measure how wide each spreads in centimetres. The thicker porridge spreads less. Write the colour, smell, thickness and taste of each. Say one way they are different.
flow.say: Look at the colour. Smell it. How thick is it? What does it taste like? Tell me one way the two porridges are different.
flow.kid: Look, smell and taste both. Write one way they are different.
flow.think: Millets grow in dry land with little water. Why might a farmer in a dry region choose to grow them?
flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, one child looks after each porridge and does the measuring, and everyone tastes both. Ragi porridge is darker, thicker and earthy in taste. Ragi has a lot of calcium, more than rice has. Rice porridge is white and mild. Millets need little water, and grow in dry land where rice cannot. Do not say that millet is better. Both are food. Say what you found.

check.q: Why are some farmers in dry regions choosing millets over rice?
options: Millets can grow with very little water
Millets grow only in rice fields
Millets need more water than rice
check.why: Rice needs a lot of water, often standing water in the field. Millets grow well in dry land with little rain. In a dry place a millet crop is more likely to succeed.

flow.context: In this step, you compare the two porridges and think about where millets grow.

projects.title: Our Family Feast: plan, cook and serve a balanced festival meal

materials.item: paper, pencils and your feast mat from Feast Builder

ingredients for 4 or 5 dishes that your family can cook, with a grown-up. Use what is already in your kitchen, so that you buy only a few things (about Rs 100 to 200 for a family) (a staple, a pulse or milk dish, two vegetable dishes, and something sweet or sour to finish)
a banana leaf (optional) or plates for serving, and small cards for the menu

projects.safety: A grown-up does the cutting, the frying and everything on the stove, and handles the hot oil. Keep young children away from the stove. Ask every guest about allergies, fasting and foods they do not eat. Wash hands before cooking.

schedule.what: Choose a festival and plan 4 or 5 dishes. Check the plan against the three jobs and the six tastes.
Make a shopping list and a menu card for each dish. Prepare what can be prepared early.
Cook with a grown-up. Serve the meal. Explain each dish to your guests.

projects.record: Keep the menu cards, a photo or drawing of the meal, and a note on which tastes and jobs your feast had and what was missing.
projects.context: In this project, you plan and cook a festival meal for your family. It must be balanced, with all three food jobs and as many of the six tastes as you can manage.

setup.art: A girl and her grandmother at a table with a feast mat, a pencil and a list of dishes, choosing what to cook.
setup.caption: 1. Plan 4 or 5 dishes. Fill your feast mat to check the jobs and the tastes.

setup.art: A shopping basket with vegetables, dal, coconut, jaggery and curd, and a hand-written menu card standing beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Shop for the ingredients, and write a menu card for each dish.

setup.art: A family sitting down to a meal on banana leaves, with a girl pointing to a menu card and explaining a dish.
setup.caption: 3. Cook and serve the meal. Explain each dish to your guests.

flow.do: Choose a festival that your family keeps, or one you would like to try. Pick 4 or 5 dishes. Write each dish on a card. Place the cards on your feast mat to check the jobs and the tastes.
flow.say: Which festival will we cook for? Which dishes will you choose? Let us put them on the mat and see which jobs and tastes are covered.
flow.kid: Pick a festival. Pick 4 or 5 dishes. Put them on your mat.

ask.q: Which job or taste is missing from your plan? What will you add?
good: I need a protective dish, a vegetable.
I have no bitter taste.
There are only sweet dishes.

flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, each child owns one dish: they plan it, write its card, help to cook it and present it. One child alone does the whole plan with a parent. Choose dishes your family can actually cook. Simple is fine: a rice dish, a dal, a vegetable, a curd dish and one sweet make a balanced festival meal. If your family fasts or avoids certain foods, plan around that.
flow.context: This is the first step of Our Family Feast. You choose the festival and the dishes.

flow.do: Look at the mat. Count the jobs and the tastes. If a box is empty or a taste is missing, change one dish. Or add a small one, such as a lemon pickle, a cucumber raita or fruit.
flow.say: Count the three job boxes. Count the tastes. What small dish could fill the gap? A pickle, a raita, a fruit?
flow.kid: Count the jobs and tastes. Add a small dish to fill any gap.

check.q: A feast has rice, pulao, puri and a sweet. Which jobs are missing?
options: Protective foods, such as vegetables and fruit, and body-building foods
Energy foods
None, since the plate is full
check.why: Rice, pulao, puri and a sweet are all mostly energy foods. A balanced feast also needs a pulse or milk dish for building and vegetables or fruit for protection.

flow.context: In this step, you check your plan and fix any gaps.

flow.do: Write a shopping list. Write a menu card for each dish with its name, where it is from, its jobs and its tastes. Prepare what can be done a day early, such as soaking dal, setting curd, or making the sweet.
flow.say: Let us write a list of what to buy. For each dish, write a small card to tell our guests what it is and what it does.
flow.kid: Write what to buy. Write a card for each dish.
flow.parent: Let your child write the cards in their own words. The cards are the point of the project. Soaking dal early is a good place to use what the Wake Up the Moong experiment showed.
flow.context: In this step, you make a shopping list and a menu card for each dish.

flow.do: Cook the dishes with a grown-up. Give your child the safe jobs: washing vegetables, mixing, grating coconut, stirring cold things and arranging the dishes. A grown-up does the stove and the knives.
flow.say: Today we cook. You will wash, mix and arrange. I will do the stove and the knife. Tell me what each dish needs.
flow.kid: Wash, mix and arrange. A grown-up does the stove and the knife.
flow.context: In this step, you cook the meal with a grown-up.
flow.parent: The child jobs take about 35 minutes. The grown-up cooking takes longer, so choose dishes that one grown-up can cook in about an hour in all, and make the sweet or curd dish a day early. Do not choose more than one fried dish.

flow.do: Serve the meal. Stand each menu card beside its dish. Ask your child to tell the family what each dish is, which job it does, and which tastes it has. Then eat together.
flow.say: Tell us about the first dish. Where is it from? What job does it do? What does it taste of?
flow.kid: Tell your family about each dish. Then eat together.
flow.think: Was every taste in the feast? Which was hard to include, and why?
flow.parent: Let the child lead. If a dish did not work, say so and laugh. A real feast has some surprises. Afterwards, write down which tastes and jobs were there, and what was missing.
flow.context: This is the last step of Our Family Feast. You serve the meal and explain each dish.

challenges.title: A Feast for Everyone: one meal, five guests
challenges.problem: Five guests are coming to a festival lunch. A grandmother eats no meat or fish, and finds hard food difficult to chew. A two-year-old cousin cannot have whole nuts or very hot food. A friend is allergic to groundnuts. Another friend eats no onion or garlic. A teenage runner needs extra energy. Plan one meal of 5 or 6 dishes that works for all five.
constraints: Every guest must be able to eat at least one dish from each of the three jobs: energy, body-building and protective.
No dish may contain groundnuts, or anything cooked in groundnut oil.
No dish may use onion or garlic.
At least five of the six tastes must be present somewhere in the meal.
Every dish must be one that a family could really cook.
materials: your feast mat and dish cards from Feast Builder
a list of the five guests and what each needs
general: Serve plain rice, a soft dal, a vegetable stir-fry, curd and a sweet. Each guest picks what suits them.
Make the dal very soft for the toddler and the grandmother, and keep a bowl of chilli powder on the side for others.
Offer a thali with a small bowl of each dish, so that anyone can skip what they cannot eat.
creative: Choose one dish that is soft and mild for everyone, such as ragi porridge or khichdi, and put the strong tastes in small side dishes.
Add a bitter dish like pavakka thoran and a sour dish like pachadi or inji puli, so that all tastes are on offer without making any single dish too strong.
Add a sesame-and-jaggery sweet if nobody has an allergy to sesame, or a fruit sweet if anyone does. Ask the guests first.
challenges.your_turn: Plan your own meal for the five guests. Write the dishes, say which guest each one suits, and show on your mat that the jobs and tastes are covered. Then ask a grown-up what they would change.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about balanced food for different people. You plan one meal that every guest can eat well.

setup.art: Five guests sitting at a table, each with a small label: vegetarian grandmother, toddler, friend with a nut allergy, friend who eats no onion or garlic, and a runner.
setup.caption: 1. Read about the five guests and write what each one needs.

setup.art: A feast mat with dish cards placed on it, and a pencil ticking each guest's name next to dishes that suit them.
setup.caption: 2. Choose dishes. For each guest, check that they can eat all three jobs.

setup.art: A finished menu on paper with a tick beside each of the six tastes and a note beside each dish saying which guest it suits.
setup.caption: 3. Check the tastes. Write the final menu.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Write the five guests on paper. Next to each one, write what they cannot eat, and what they need more of.
flow.say: Five guests are coming. Let us write what each one cannot eat and what each one needs.
flow.kid: Write the five guests. Write what each one needs and cannot eat.

ask.q: Which guest is hardest to plan for, and why?
good: The toddler, because of the nuts and the hot spices.
The runner, who needs more energy.
The friend who eats no onion or garlic, because so many dishes use them.

flow.parent: A toddler of two should not be given whole nuts or hard chunks, because they can choke. Honey is not safe for babies under one year. Allergies can be serious, so when you cook for real guests, ask them or their parents first. For this paper challenge, treat the rules as given.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Feast for Everyone. You list what each guest needs.

flow.do: Choose 5 or 6 dishes from your cards or from your own family's recipes. Place them on your mat. Next to each dish, write which guests can eat it.
flow.say: Pick dishes for the meal. For each one, who can eat it? Is there a dish for each guest in every job?
flow.kid: Pick 5 or 6 dishes. Write who can eat each one.

check.q: A dish of dal with a spoon of groundnut chutney on top is on the menu. What should you do?
options: Change it, or serve the chutney separately, since one guest is allergic to groundnuts
Keep it, because only a little groundnut is there
Tell the guest to eat around it
check.why: A groundnut allergy can be serious even with a small amount. The safest choice is to leave groundnut out of the meal altogether, and keep anything that has touched it away from that guest's plate.

flow.context: In this step, you choose the dishes and check them against each guest.

flow.do: Colour the six taste circles for the whole menu. If any is missing, change a dish or add a small one. Write the final menu with a note on each dish.
flow.say: Which tastes are on the menu now? Which are missing? What small dish could fill the gap?
flow.kid: Colour the taste circles. Add a small dish for any missing taste.
flow.context: In this step, you check all six tastes and fix any gaps.

flow.do: Show your menu to a grown-up. Ask what they would change. Write down one thing you would change after hearing them.
flow.say: Show your menu to someone. Ask what they would change. Do you agree with them?
flow.kid: Show your menu to a grown-up. Write one change you would make.
flow.think: Is a meal fair if only some guests can eat all of it?
flow.parent: A good menu does not make anyone a special case at the table. If every guest can find something from each job on the same table, the meal works. Listen to the child's reasons before suggesting changes.
flow.context: This is the last step of A Feast for Everyone. You share your menu and listen to another view.

items.p: Which sentence best describes a balanced diet?
opts: Many different foods eaten over days, so the body gets all the nutrients it needs
One perfect plate at every single meal
Only the foods that people call healthy
items.why: What matters is what you eat over days and weeks, not at a single meal. Many kinds of food together give all the nutrients. Choosing only 'healthy' foods can still leave out some groups.

items.p: Each taste is sensed only in its own zone of the tongue.
items.why: False. Taste buds for every taste are spread over the tongue. The zones differ only a little in how strongly they sense each taste. The old tongue map was a mistake.

items.p: A small group of taste cells on the tongue is called a taste ____.
items.why: A taste bud is a group of 50 to 100 taste cells packed together like segments of an orange. You have thousands of them.

items.p: Match each food to the job it mostly does in the body.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Rice and ghee are rich in starch and fat, so they give energy. Dal and curd are rich in protein, which builds the body. Palak is rich in vitamins and minerals, which protect the body.

items.p: Sort each food by the taste it mainly gives.
items.a: as given
items.why: Jaggery and honey have sugar, which tastes sweet. Tamarind and lemon have acids, which taste sour. Karela and neem have bitter chemicals.

items.p: A green chilli makes your mouth feel hot. What does science say this heat is?
opts: A signal of heat and pain from nerves, not one of the five tastes
The sixth basic taste
A sweet taste in disguise
items.why: Chilli heat is felt by nerves that sense heat and pain. Science lists five tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Ayurveda counts pungent as one of its six rasas.

items.p: A glass of sweet fizzy drink and a ripe mango send the same sweet signal to the tongue.
items.why: True. The tongue senses sugar and reports sweet. It cannot tell whether fibre, vitamins and water come with the sugar. The mango gives them, and the fizzy drink gives almost none.

items.p: In a blind taste test, a tester does 16 touches. The taste is named wrongly 3 times. How many touches were named correctly?
items.why: 16 take away 3 is 13. So 13 touches were named correctly. A wrong answer is still a result, because it shows how often a tester guesses.

items.p: A friend says that sweet is only tasted at the tip of the tongue. What would you say to your friend? Use what you found in the blind taste test.
items.a: I would say that is the old tongue map, and it is wrong. In our test, sweet was named correctly on the tip, the edges and the back. Taste buds for every taste are spread across the tongue. Some zones are a little more sensitive, but none are blind to a taste.
items.why: A strong answer names the evidence from the test, that every taste was sensed in every zone. It may also say that small differences in strength are not the same as separate zones.

items.p: A thali has rice, roti, puri and halwa. Which food jobs are missing?
opts: Body-building foods and protective foods
Energy foods
None, because the thali is full
items.why: Rice, roti, puri and halwa are all mostly energy foods. The thali also needs dal, curd or another pulse or milk food for building, and vegetables or fruit for protection.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Ragi, jowar, bajra, rice.
items.a: Rice, because the other three are millets.
items.why: Ragi, jowar and bajra are millets, small-seeded grains that grow well in dry land. Rice is a different grain that needs much more water.

items.p: Soaked moong seeds weigh more than dry moong because they have taken in ____.
items.why: A dry seed has very little water. Seeds soak up water through their skin and swell. The extra weight is the water.

items.p: Draw a plate for a festival meal that has all three food jobs. Label each food with its job.
items.a: A plate with at least one energy food such as rice or roti, one body-building food such as dal or curd, and one protective food such as a vegetable or fruit, each labelled.
items.why: A strong drawing shows all three jobs on the one plate and labels them correctly. Two dishes may share a job, and one dish may do more than one job.

items.p: Why can many festival sweets, like laddu, be kept for weeks?
opts: They have very little water, so microbes cannot grow in them
They are always kept in a fridge
They are cooked with a lot of water
items.why: Microbes need water to grow. A laddu is made of sugar, flour, ghee and nuts, with very little water in it, so spoilage microbes grow very slowly.

items.p: A laddu at Diwali fits in a balanced diet, but a laddu at every meal would not. Why not?
items.a: A laddu is rich in sugar and ghee, so it gives a lot of energy and few other nutrients. A balanced diet is a pattern over many days. One laddu on a special day is a small part of the pattern. Laddus at every meal would crowd out dal, vegetables and fruit.
items.why: A strong answer says that a balanced diet is a pattern, and that one festival sweet is a small part of it. It may also say that eating it every day would leave less room for other foods.

items.p: A balanced meal must look the same in every part of India.
items.why: False. A Kerala sadya, a Gujarati thali and a Naga meal are all different. Each joins a staple, a pulse or fish or milk food, and vegetables, using what grows nearby.

items.p: Which taste is on the science list of five basic tastes, but is not one of the six rasas?
opts: Umami
Pungent
Astringent
items.why: Umami is the savoury taste of foods like ripe tomato and mushroom. Ayurveda's six rasas are sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent. Pungent and astringent are feelings, not tastes.

items.p: In 1942, a chart showed small differences in how strongly each part of the tongue senses a taste. The chart was then turned into a map of separate zones. What was the mistake?
opts: Small differences in strength were read as separate zones
Taste buds were found only on the tip
People could not taste at all
items.why: Hänig's numbers in 1901 showed only small differences. When they were drawn as a map, each taste seemed to have its own zone. Careful tests in 1974 showed every zone senses every taste.

items.p: A taste cell lives as long as the person who owns it.
items.why: False. A taste cell lives only about ten days to two weeks, and then a new one grows. Your sense of taste is being rebuilt all the time.

items.p: Lemon and tamarind taste sour because they hold ____.
items.why: Sour is the taste of acids. Lemon, tamarind, curd and unripe mango all have acid in them.

items.p: Match each taste to what it may be telling you about the food.
pairs: there is sugar, a quick fuel
there is acid, as in unripe fruit
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are ideas about why we have taste. Scientists treat them as ideas, not as proven facts. Taste is not a perfect guide, because some bitter foods are safe, and some poisons taste sweet.

items.p: Put the steps of the Wake Up the Moong test in the right order.
a: Weigh three equal portions of dry moong
Soak two of the portions overnight
Drain and weigh them, and let one bowl sprout
Cook all three together and test one seed from each bag every 5 minutes
Compare the weights and the cooking times
items.why: The soaking and sprouting come before the cooking, because the cooking test compares the three kinds of seed. All three batches must be cooked in the same way so that the test is fair.

items.p: Dry moong took 36 minutes to turn soft. Soaked moong took 18 minutes and sprouted moong took 9 minutes. How many times as long did the dry moong take as the sprouted moong?
items.a: 4 times
items.why: 36 divided by 9 is 4. The dry moong took 4 times as long as the sprouted moong, which fits the idea that sprouting has already started to soften the seed.

items.p: Sort each way of preparing or eating food by its main effect.
cats: Helps the body take in iron
items: a squeeze of lemon on palak
Helps the body take in iron
strong tea drunk with a meal
items.a: as given
items.why: Phytic acid holds on to iron and zinc, and soaking, sprouting and fermenting break it down. Vitamin C in lemon helps the gut take in iron from plant foods. Tea can lower how much iron the body takes in.

items.p: A packet of millet biscuits has the word 'superfood' on the front. The first two ingredients are sugar and palm oil.

views.says: Our biscuits have real millet in them. Millet is an old, healthy grain, so our biscuits are a good choice.
Millet is good food. But biscuits that are mostly sugar and oil are not a health food, whatever grain is in them. Read the ingredients.

views.who: A farmer who grows ragi (an imagined view)
views.says: I am glad people want millet again. I would rather they bought the grain or the flour, and cooked it at home.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What evidence would help you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view, gives a reason and refers to what is in the biscuits, for example that sugar and oil come first on the list.
items.why: 'Superfood' is a selling word, not a science word. The ingredients on a label are listed from most to least by weight, so sugar and oil being first means there is more of them than of millet.

items.p: Why does a sweet fizzy drink give a sweet taste without the goodness of a mango?
items.a: The tongue senses sugar and reports sweet. It cannot tell what else is in the food. A mango has sugar together with fibre, vitamins and water. A fizzy drink has sugar and almost nothing else. So both taste sweet, but only the mango gives the goodness.
items.why: A strong answer says that taste is a signal from a chemical, and that the same signal can come with or without the other nutrients.

items.p: Two cousins taste the same piece of karela. One says it is very bitter and the other says it is a little bitter. What is the best explanation?
opts: Their taste sensors differ a little because of genes and past experience
One of them must be telling a lie
The karela changed between the two bites
items.why: People have slightly different genes for bitter sensors, and the foods they grew up on also change how strong a taste feels. So the same food can taste different to two people.

items.p: Free school meals can bring more children to school as well as feeding them.
items.why: True. Studies of school meals in India have found that more children come to school when a meal is served. Tamil Nadu began giving school meals in the 1950s, and a national scheme now reaches children across India.

items.p: A family eats rice, rice flakes and potato at most meals. Which change would improve their balance most?
opts: Add dal or other pulses, vegetables, curd or milk, and fruit
Eat more rice so nobody is hungry
Stop eating rice completely
items.why: Rice, rice flakes and potato are all energy foods. The family's diet lacks building foods and protective foods. Adding them is better than removing the rice, which is still a useful staple.

items.p: Draw a bowl of Ugadi pachadi with its six ingredients. Label the taste of each one.
items.a: A bowl with six labelled ingredients: jaggery (sweet), tamarind (sour), salt (salty), neem flowers (bitter), pepper (pungent) and raw mango (astringent).
items.why: The pachadi holds all six rasas. A strong drawing labels each ingredient with its taste, and may note that pungent and astringent are feelings and not tastes.

items.p: Old cooks soaked dal and fermented batter long before anyone knew about phytic acid. How can people find out that something works before they know why?
items.a: People can try a thing many times and notice what happens. If a family soaks dal and everyone does better, they keep doing it. Later, scientists can test it and find the reason. Knowing that it works and knowing why are two different steps.
items.why: A strong answer says that noticing a pattern comes before explaining it. It may also say that a test can show whether the old way really works, or whether it only seems to.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Ugadi pachadi, shukto, pavakka thoran, payasam.
items.a: Payasam, because it is sweet, and the other three each have a bitter taste.
items.why: Ugadi pachadi has neem flowers, shukto has a little karela, and pavakka thoran is made of karela. Payasam is a sweet milk dish.

items.p: Design a fair blind test to find out whether people can tell a spoon of sugar water from a spoon of apple juice with the same sweetness. Say what you keep the same and what you change.
items.a: I would put the sugar water and the apple juice in two cups the same size, with the same amount in each, and let the tester shut their eyes. A helper would shuffle the cups so the tester does not know which is which. The only thing I change is which liquid it is. I keep the temperature, the amount and the spoon the same. I would test many people and write down how often they are right.
items.why: A strong answer keeps everything the same except the one thing being tested, hides which cup is which from the tester, and tests more than once. A control of two identical cups would also be a good idea.

items.p: A friend tests her own tongue with her eyes open and with no plain water cup. Which problem matters most?
opts: She can see which cup is which, so her answers are not blind
She used cups instead of bowls
She rinsed her mouth between tests
items.why: If the tester can see the cup, she may name the taste she expects and not the taste she feels. Hiding the cups, and adding plain water, makes the test fair. Rinsing is a good idea, not a problem.

items.p: Ayurveda says a good meal holds all six tastes. A nutrition scientist says a body needs nutrients, which are measured, and not tasted.

views.says: The six tastes are a simple way for a cook to check a meal. A meal with every taste is rarely one-sided.
A meal can have all six tastes and still lack iron. We must measure nutrients, because a tongue cannot measure them.

views.who: A cook in a school kitchen (an imagined view)
views.says: I use the tastes to plan a meal that children will eat. I use the food groups to plan a meal that is balanced. I need both.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What evidence would help you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view and gives a reason, for example that tastes are a good guide for a cook, but nutrients must still be checked.
items.why: Both views have something right. Tastes are a convenient guide, but they do not measure nutrients. The cook uses both, which is often how real planning works.

items.p: A festival feast has 15 dishes. One third are protective, and one third are body-building. How many are energy foods?
items.why: One third of 15 is 5. So 5 are protective and 5 are body-building. That leaves 15 take away 10, which is 5 energy foods. The feast has an equal number of each job.

items.p: A sweet like mysore pak keeps for weeks. Which fact explains this best?
opts: It is made of sugar, flour and ghee with almost no water
It is cooked at a very high heat
It is wrapped in leaves
items.why: Microbes need water to grow. A food with sugar and fat but little water gives them almost nothing to work with, so it keeps. Heat during cooking does not protect food once it has cooled.

items.p: A neighbour says, 'When I crave biscuits, it means my body needs them.' What would you say, using what you know about taste?
items.a: A craving is a wish for a taste. Our body does have a real hunger for salt when we are short of it. But a craving for sugar, salt and fat in a packet is often habit, because factory food is made to be hard to stop. The biscuit gives the taste signal but not much else. So a craving does not always mean the body needs the food.
items.why: A strong answer separates a taste signal from a need. It may say that some cravings, such as for salt, can be real, and that others come from habit and factory food.

items.p: Because pongal is a traditional food, it can be eaten at every meal without any limit.
items.why: False. Sakkarai pongal is rich in sugar and ghee, which is why it is a festival dish. A traditional food is not automatically right for every day. The pattern over days matters.

items.p: Match each festival to the foods of its season.
pairs: new rice, moong dal and jaggery
Makar Sankranti in the cool months
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Festival foods follow what the land gives in each part of the year. Rice is harvested around Pongal, raw mango and neem come in spring, and sesame is eaten in the cool months.

items.p: Taste scientists count five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and ____.
items.why: Umami is the savoury taste, made by glutamate. It was named by the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda in 1908, from the taste of kombu seaweed.

items.p: A hungry child gets a midday meal of rice, dal and a vegetable. Why might this meal matter more to her than to a child who eats well at home?
items.a: If her family has little money, this may be her biggest and best meal of the day. It gives energy from the rice, building food from the dal and protection from the vegetable. A child who eats well at home already gets these foods, so the school meal adds less.
items.why: A strong answer says that the school meal fills a gap. It may mention that a balanced meal is not equally available to every child, and that this is a question of fairness.

items.p: Which lunch best suits a guest who eats no meat, no onion and no garlic, and is allergic to groundnuts?
opts: Rice, dal with cumin and ginger, a coconut vegetable stir-fry, curd and fruit
Dal tadka with garlic and fried onion
Rice with groundnut chutney and curd
items.why: The first meal has energy from rice, building food from dal and curd, and protection from vegetables and fruit, without meat, onion, garlic or groundnut. The other two break at least one rule.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Idli batter, curd, mishti doi, sabudana khichdi.
items.a: Sabudana khichdi, because it is not fermented. The other three are made by microbes.
items.why: Idli batter, curd and mishti doi are all changed by living microbes. Sabudana khichdi is made from sago pearls cooked with peanuts and potato, and no fermentation is needed.

items.p: Draw three moong seeds in a row: a dry one, a soaked one and a sprouted one. Label what is different about each.
items.a: A small hard seed labelled dry, a larger swollen seed labelled soaked, and a swollen seed with a small white tail labelled sprouted.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the seed getting bigger as the seed takes in water, and the tail, which is the first root, on the sprouted one.

items.p: Sort each statement by whether the blind taste test supports it.
items: Sour can be tasted on the tip of the tongue
Bitter can be tasted only at the back
Salty can be tasted on the edges of the tongue
Sweet can be tasted only at the tip
items.a: as given
items.why: In the test, every taste was named in every zone. So the statements that say a taste is sensed in one place only are not supported.

items.p: Where does a meal end and you begin? Use what you know about food, cells and taste to give your view.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer may say that the rice in a meal becomes part of the body within days, so the meal does not end at the mouth. It may also say that the taste cells that sense the meal are themselves rebuilt from earlier meals. It may leave the question open, with a reason.
items.why: This is an open question with no single answer. A strong answer gives a view, uses evidence from the unit, and stays honest about what is not known.

quiz.p: A girl eats only rice and ghee every day and always feels full. What is the best way to describe her diet?
opts: Not balanced, because it leaves out many groups of food
Balanced, because it fills her stomach
Balanced, because ghee is healthy
quiz.why: Feeling full is not the same as getting every nutrient. Rice and ghee are both energy foods. A balanced diet also needs building foods and protective foods over the days.

quiz.p: Where on the tongue can you taste sour?
opts: Anywhere there are taste buds
Only on the sides
Only at the back
quiz.why: Taste buds for every taste are found all over the tongue. The old map that put sour only on the sides was a mistake.

quiz.p: In the blind taste test, what is the job of the cup of plain water?
opts: It checks whether the tester is really tasting or only guessing
It makes the other cups taste weaker
It gives the tester a drink
quiz.why: Plain water is the control. If the tester names a taste for it, the test shows that some answers may be guesses.

quiz.p: Which of these is not one of the five basic tastes found by science?
opts: Pungent
Umami
Bitter
quiz.why: Pungent is the hot feeling of chilli and pepper, sensed by nerves of heat and pain. Umami and bitter are basic tastes sensed by taste cells.

quiz.p: Why do sprouted moong seeds cook faster than dry moong seeds?
opts: They have taken in water and started to grow, so the seeds are softer inside
They are a different kind of seed
They are cooked on a hotter flame
quiz.why: In a fair test, the seed and the flame are the same. Soaking lets water in, and sprouting starts the seed breaking down the stored food, so the seed softens sooner.

quiz.p: A mango and a sweet fizzy drink both taste sweet. What is the main difference between them?
opts: The mango has fibre and vitamins with its sugar, and the drink has almost none
The mango has no sugar in it
The tongue can tell which one is healthier
quiz.why: The tongue only reports sweet. It cannot tell what else comes with the sugar. A mango gives fibre, water and vitamins, and a fizzy drink gives sugar and very little else.

quiz.p: A thali has rice, dal, a vegetable and curd. What does the dal mainly do for the body?
opts: It helps build the body
It mostly gives energy
It does nothing the rice does not do
quiz.why: Dal is rich in protein, which the body uses to grow and mend. Rice is the main energy food in this thali. The two do different jobs.

quiz.p: Why is Ugadi pachadi made with raw mango and neem flowers?
opts: They are in season in spring, when Ugadi falls
They are the only foods that taste bitter and sour
They are the cheapest foods in the market all year
quiz.why: Festival foods often follow the season. Raw mango and neem flowers appear in spring. Their tastes also fit the idea of a bowl with all six tastes.

quiz.p: Which action helps the body take in iron from dal and palak?
opts: A squeeze of lemon on the meal
Drinking strong tea with the meal
Eating the meal very fast
quiz.why: Vitamin C in lemon helps the gut take in iron from plant foods. Tea drunk with a meal can lower how much iron is taken in.

quiz.p: Why might two people taste the same piece of karela and disagree about how bitter it is?
opts: Their taste sensors and past experiences differ a little
One of them is imagining it
Karela tastes different each time it is cut
quiz.why: Genes for bitter sensors vary from person to person, and the foods a child grows up eating change how a taste feels. Both people are tasting honestly.

quiz.p: Which meal best suits a guest who eats no meat and needs energy for a long run?
opts: Rice, dal, a vegetable, curd and a banana
A packet of chips and a fizzy drink
Only a cup of tea
quiz.why: The first meal gives energy from the rice and banana, building food from dal and curd, and protection from the vegetable, with no meat. The other two give little besides sugar, salt and fat.

quiz.p: In a week's food diary, the row for protective foods is very short. What does this tell you?
opts: This week had few vegetables and fruits, so add some next week
The family has done something wrong and must be told off
Protective foods are not needed
quiz.why: A short row is information about the week, not a mistake. The next step is to add some of that group in a way the family enjoys.

maths.problem: In a blind taste test, a tester names the taste correctly in 14 of 16 touches. What fraction of the touches were correct? Is that more than three quarters?
maths.answer: 14 out of 16, which is 7 out of 8. Yes, it is more than three quarters.
maths.explain: Three quarters of 16 is 12, because 16 divided by 4 is 4, and 4 times 3 is 12. The tester named 14 correctly, which is more than 12. 14 out of 16 is the same as 7 out of 8, because both numbers can be halved.
maths.context: In the Blind Taste Test, you make 20 touches and count how many answers were correct. A fraction lets you compare tests with different numbers of touches.
maths.why_maths: The fraction of touches that were right lets you compare two testers, even when they did a different number of touches.

maths.problem: This is a made-up example. 50 grams of dry moong weighs 115 grams after soaking. How many grams of water did the seeds take in? Is that more than half of the soaked weight?
maths.answer: 65 grams of water. Yes, it is more than half.
maths.explain: 115 take away 50 is 65. Half of 115 is 57 and a half. 65 is more than 57 and a half, so more than half of the soaked weight is water.
maths.context: In the Wake Up the Moong test, you weigh seeds before and after soaking. Subtraction tells you how much water the seeds took in.
maths.why_maths: Taking the weight before from the weight after tells you how much the seeds gained, which is the water.

maths.problem: In a made-up test, dry moong takes 36 minutes to turn soft, soaked moong takes 18 minutes, and sprouted moong takes 9 minutes. How many times as long does dry moong take as sprouted? How many minutes do you save by sprouting?
maths.answer: 4 times as long. You save 27 minutes.
maths.explain: 36 divided by 9 is 4, so the dry moong takes 4 times as long. 36 take away 9 is 27 minutes saved. The sprouted moong halves the soaked time again, since 18 divided by 2 is 9.
maths.context: In the Wake Up the Moong test, you time how long each batch takes to cook. Division tells you how many times longer one took than another.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one time by another shows how many times as long the slow batch took, which is easier to picture than two separate numbers.

maths.problem: In a food diary, one picture stands for 2 servings. Energy foods have 7 pictures, body-building foods have 4, protective foods have 2 and snacks have 3. How many servings of protective food did the child eat? How many more servings of energy food than protective food?
maths.answer: 4 servings of protective food. 10 more servings of energy food.
maths.explain: 2 pictures of 2 servings each is 4 servings of protective food. Energy has 7 pictures of 2, which is 14 servings. 14 take away 4 is 10 more servings of energy food.
maths.context: In the Seven-Day Food Diary, you draw a pictograph of your week. One picture stands for 2 servings.
maths.why_maths: A pictograph shows at a glance which group is long and which is short, and you multiply by what one picture stands for to find the real number.

maths.problem: A festival feast has 12 dishes: 5 energy foods, 3 body-building foods and 4 protective foods. What fraction of the dishes are protective? If the planner wants an equal number of each job, how many dishes of each job would that be?
maths.answer: 4 out of 12, which is one third. Four dishes of each job.
maths.explain: 4 out of 12 is the same as 1 out of 3, because both numbers divide by 4. An equal split of 12 dishes between 3 jobs is 12 divided by 3, which is 4 each.
maths.context: In Feast Builder and Our Family Feast, you count how many dishes belong to each food job. A fraction shows whether the feast is balanced.
maths.why_maths: The fraction of dishes in each job shows whether a feast is lopsided, and how many dishes to change.

maths.problem: A packet says ragi has about 350 milligrams of calcium in every 100 grams, and polished rice has about 10 milligrams in every 100 grams. How many times as much calcium does ragi have? How many grams of ragi hold 700 milligrams of calcium?
maths.answer: 35 times as much. 200 grams of ragi.
maths.explain: 350 divided by 10 is 35, so ragi has 35 times as much calcium. 700 is twice 350, so you need twice 100 grams, which is 200 grams of ragi.
maths.context: In Millet Hunt, you read a packet of ragi flour and cook a ragi porridge. These round numbers are close to the values in the Indian food tables.
maths.why_maths: A ratio shows how many times bigger one amount is than another, and doubling the amount of food doubles the amount of calcium.

maths.problem: Suppose a child eats about 1,600 kilocalories a day. Advice from the World Health Organization is that sugar added to food and drink should be less than one tenth of that energy. One gram of sugar gives about 4 kilocalories. What is the most added sugar, in grams, the child should have in one day? A 250 millilitre bottle of a sweet drink has 10 grams of sugar in every 100 millilitres. Is the sugar in the bottle more than half of the day's limit?
maths.answer: 160 kilocalories, which is 40 grams of sugar. The bottle has 25 grams, which is more than half of 40.
maths.explain: One tenth of 1,600 is 160 kilocalories. 160 divided by 4 is 40 grams. 250 millilitres is 2 and a half times 100 millilitres, so the bottle holds 2 and a half times 10 grams, which is 25 grams. Half of 40 is 20, and 25 is more than 20.
maths.context: The card 'A taste can be copied without the goodness' explains how a sweet drink gives sugar without the goodness of fruit. Here you check how much a bottle takes from a day's limit.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying and dividing turns advice about a tenth of the day's energy into grams of sugar, so that you can check a label against it.

open_questions.q: Why do some people love bitter foods like karela while others cannot bear them?
open_questions.why_open: Genes explain part of it, and the foods a child grows up with explain part. Scientists do not yet know how much each part matters, or how a child's liking can change.

open_questions.q: Is fat a sixth basic taste?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists found sensors for fatty acids on the tongue and have proposed a taste for fat. Others say the evidence is not yet strong enough to add it to the list.

open_questions.q: Do the six rasas of Ayurveda match anything that can be measured in the body?
open_questions.why_open: Some of the rasas, like sweet and bitter, match tastes that science has measured. Others, like pungent and astringent, are feelings. How far the old system lines up with the new one is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Does eating a very wide variety of plants make the gut healthier?
open_questions.why_open: A large study in 2018 found that people who ate more than 30 kinds of plant a week had more kinds of microbe in their gut. Nobody yet knows how much this changes health.

open_questions.q: How much of what we like to eat is learned before we are born, and how much is born into us?
open_questions.why_open: Julie Mennella found that babies prefer flavours they met in the womb and in their mother's milk. But how long this lasts, and how much a child's liking can change later, is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Why do people everywhere mark special days with special food?
open_questions.why_open: Historians and scientists have ideas about sharing, memory and belonging, but nobody can say for certain where the habit began.

quiz: Every taste can be sensed on every part of the tongue that has taste buds.
Taste cells for all tastes are spread over the tongue, so the old tongue map is wrong.
Sweet is tasted only at the tip of the tongue, and bitter only at the back.
Taste buds for every taste are found all over the tongue, and also in the mouth and throat.
A balanced diet is judged over many days and weeks, not by one single meal.
Different foods give different nutrients, so the mix across days is what counts.
Traditional food is always healthier than modern food.
Some traditional diets lacked nutrients; for example, mostly polished rice gives very little thiamine.
If you crave a sweet snack, your body must need what is in it.
Most cravings come from habit, mood and factory foods made to be hard to stop.
Soaking and sprouting pulses can make their iron and zinc easier for the body to absorb.
These old ways of preparing food make the minerals inside plant foods easier to take in.
Eating a laddu at a festival means your diet is no longer balanced.
Balance is a pattern over weeks, and a festival sweet fits into a mostly varied diet.
A sweet drink can give a sweet taste signal without giving the goodness of fruit.
Taste is a signal from chemicals, and a food can copy the signal without the goodness that used to come with it.
Millets are a new superfood that can fix a whole diet on their own.
Millets are very old grains, and no single food gives the body everything it needs.
India grows enough food, yet many children still lack iron and other nutrients.
Enough food in total does not mean everyone gets enough of the right foods.
odd: Ragi, jowar and bajra are small-seeded millets that grow in dry land; rice is not a millet.
Sweet, sour and bitter are tastes; science counts the burning of pepper as a feeling of heat and pain.
The first three make minerals in plant foods easier for the body to take in; frying does not.
Rice, wheat and ragi are staple grains that give most of the day's energy; spinach is a leafy vegetable.
The first three are kinds of malnutrition; eating many different foods is what a balanced diet needs.
